0e2c68e3-b598-43fb-ba17-d0048c67f11f: In this immersive workshop, we explore the deeper esoteric meanings within the poetry of Indian mystic saints such as Kabir and Guru Nanak through the indigenous folk songs of the Malwa region of Central India. These songs belong to a living oral tradition that has been carried forward for over 600 years. Priyal will guide us through this journey by singing and interpreting these songs while accompanying himself on traditional instruments like the Tambura and Kartaal. Printed translations will be provided, allowing participants to follow along and join in the singing if they wish. After each song, we will pause for reflection, creating space for participants to share whatever arises within them. We will also spend time in shared silence, gently turning inward to experience the stillness pointed to in the songs. Priyal will also share stories from the life of Kabir, insights into India’s oral traditions, and reflections on his own journey — how he encountered his Guru and how these teachings have shaped his life. Through song, storytelling, collective reflection, and silence, this workshop invites us to touch something deeper within ourselves — a space where boundaries soften, and a sense of oneness with each other and the world begins to emerge. About Priyal Maheshwari: Priyal Maheshwari is a musician and yoga teacher whose journey bridges the worlds of science, spirituality, and the arts. After graduating from Indian Institute of Technology, Kharagpur and spending six years in the IT industry, he felt an inner calling to step away from the corporate path and dedicate his life to the transformative power of music and wellness practices. Through his work, Priyal integrates music, yoga, and meditation as tools for healing and self-discovery. His approach helps people reconnect with the deeper aspects of their being and cultivate a more balanced, integrated way of living. Alongside extensive training in classical music, Priyal has immersed himself in the oral traditions of saint poets such as Kabir, Nanak, and Meera. He continues to learn directly from PadmaShri Prahlad Singh Tipanya ji, one of the foremost carriers of Kabir’s singing tradition from the Malwa region of Central India. These teachings have deeply shaped Priyal’s own musical journey, grounding it in devotion, simplicity, and the timeless wisdom of the saints. Priyal regularly shares his music in concerts, satsangs, and community gatherings. He also organizes retreats and collaborative events with Prahlad ji and his ensemble, creating spaces where participants can experience the confluence of music, spirituality, and collective harmony.

28ef01f3-fc82-4a68-92f8-a0f336302c5b: Elephant Gym successfully completed a world tour spanning 60 cities across 23 countries. However, behind this achievement lay an unseen crisis of disbandment, along with hidden conflicts and struggles. What does it truly mean to be a band? The film was first screened in October 2025 at the Kaohsiung Film Festival, one of Taiwan’s leading film festivals, and will also be shown in theaters in both Japan and Taiwan. While their world tour across 23 countries and 60 cities was a major success, the film reveals the untold story behind it—including a looming breakup crisis during its preparation, as well as the band’s internal conflicts and struggles. “If your dreams were to become reality, what price would you be willing to pay?“ Elephant Gym, an instrumental band from Kaohsiung, Taiwan, has been creating indie music since its formation in 2012. Their sound blends complex rhythms with irregular time signatures and sophisticated melodies. In Taiwan, their avant-garde musical style often raised the question: who would even listen to this? However, in 2024, they embarked on a world tour covering 23 countries and 60 shows, including three performances in the Philippines. They captivated audiences worldwide and firmly established their presence. Yet behind the glamorous stage, there were deep struggles. Between guitarist Tell Chang and bassist KT Chang—who are siblings—there were conflicts between family ties and band dynamics. Drummer Chia-Chin Tu had to make the difficult decision to leave another band. And just before the world tour, the band faced a crisis that nearly led to their breakup—filled with unseen pain and clashes. Still, they chose to believe in their music and in their bond, and continued moving forward. From a niche genre to the global stage, Elephant Gym asks through their musical journey: What is a band made of people with different backgrounds? What does it mean for people to connect? Between dreams and reality, they found their own “truth.” Come witness that answer in theaters. Band member Q&A (over Zoom) to follow the screening! 3f6e747c-a018-44fc-a26c-51ae30cb9a18: Please join us for a discussion with the author of No to Nuclear: Why Nuclear Power Destroys Lives, Derails Climate Progress and Provokes War . Linda Pentz Gunter and Eric Wolfe speak in conversation on Sunday, October 11th at 7 pm. Trump is pushing for nuclear power expansion, to enrich himself and his billionaire tech friends. But does anyone else really benefit? In No To Nuclea r, Pentz Gunter moves beyond the science and statistics, centering the stories of the Nuclear Age around the inherent colonialism and corruption of the nuclear industry and the Indigenous communities who have been preyed upon for profit and left to pay a terrible price. She takes us to Native American and First Nations communities, to the nomadic Tuareg of Niger and Aboriginal lands in Australia, where Black, Brown and Indigenous communities, far from the countries who profit, have been forced to mine the uranium that fuels the nuclear industry. She finds similar stories where atomic bombs have been tested, in the Marshall Islands and French Polynesia. And she reminds us that animals, who we disregard so cruelly, are harmed, too. Finally, the book urges us to rediscover the beauty and the miracle that is Planet Earth and to embrace justice first, if we are to have a chance to prevent the worst of the climate crisis and avoid nuclear war. Linda Pentz Gunter is the founder and executive director of the US-based non-profit Beyond Nuclear. She also created and writes for her organization's news platform, Beyond Nuclear International. A former full-time journalist, she continues to contribute feature stories to the Morning Star (UK) and Ralph Nader's Capitol Hill Citizen . Eric Wolfe has been active in peace, environment, and labor issues for 60 years. He helped organize the Clamshell Alliance in 1976 to oppose construction of the Seabrook reactors. Through his puppet show, Burnt Toast: Trouble in the Nation’s Breadbasket , he advocated for non-violent direct action against nuclear power in 20 states, including California. Acres of Clams , his feature-length documentary about the Clamshell Alliance, was released in 2024. Eric has lived in San Francisco since 1988 with his wife, science writer Susan Freinkel.

566d98d5-dfec-4976-8210-363c1c9afc99: Renowned psychotherapist and astrologer Debra Silverman offers an accessible guide to the life-changing benefits of astrology, combining wisdom from both fields to help readers remember the truth of their soul's expression through the eyes of self-love. This paperback edition will feature a special limited purple cover, while supplies last! In a chaotic, confusing, and divisive world, Debra Silverman introduces astrology as the medicine for accepting our human nature--its idiosyncrasies and dilemmas. Through an application of both therapy and astrology, this breakthrough guide equips readers with tools that release self-judgment, inner criticism, negativity, and misunderstanding. Every sign struggles with psychological issues. Understanding the unique topics relative to your sign, it’s no surprise you are quirky. Learning how to accept who you are and love yourself unconditionally through the lens of astrology is at the heart of this book. Debra Silverman teaches you how to step away from the struggle of your ego and see yourself with the calm objectivity of your soul. You will learn to love what you see—not just your best qualities but everything about you. She shows you how to aim for the high road of your personality. Most of all, you will cultivate compassion for all the other signs in the zodiac. Learn the meaning of the sun, moon, rising sign, Mercury, and Saturn. Using Debra’s method combining the wisdom of astrology and psychology, readers will remember the truth of their soul’s expression, seen through the eyes of self-love. “A lovely piece of writing, light on its feet, landing blows when they are needed, comforting when required but never pulling punches.” —Sting “I have a feeling it might open your heart and mind to parts of yourself you’ve yet to discover.” —Julianne Hough, bestselling author, entertainer, and entrepreneur “A sparkling gem... This is essential reading for these times!” —Colette Baron-Reid, bestselling oracle expert, author, and artist "In a sea of books on astrology, Debra’s stands out." —Gabby Bernstein, #1 New York Times bestselling author of The Universe Has Your Back Debra Silverman is an astrologer, psychotherapist-trained educator, and author who has spent nearly five decades building a disciplined, system-based approach to astrology rooted in temperament, pattern recognition, and human behavior. At a moment when astrology is both ubiquitous and flattened into algorithmic shorthand, Silverman has become one of the field’s most consequential institutional voices, known for codifying chart literacy into frameworks that can be taught, applied, and carried forward across relationships, work, and personal change. Silverman’s work is anchored in clinical training and long practice. She earned a Bachelor’s degree in Psychology and Dance from York University and a Master’s degree in Clinical Psychology from Antioch University, then built a career working with individuals, couples, and families while developing a methodology that treats the birth chart as a structured vocabulary rather than entertainment. Her signature emphasis on the Four Elements gives audiences a clear entry point into temperament, conflict style, and stress response, translating complex archetypal material into language that holds up in conversation and decision-making. In 2016, she founded Debra Silverman Astrology, formalizing her methodology into a global education platform spanning multi-level curriculum, mentorship, retreats and intensives, and advanced practitioner training. At the center is Applied Astrology School, a structured program that has trained thousands of students worldwide, supported by trained mentors and advanced cohorts. Silverman also developed the 4E process, an elements-based methodology practiced through individualized sessions and certification retreats by trained facilitators, extending her work beyond instruction into a defined practice model. Within contemporary astrology, Silverman is widely regarded as a trusted authority for method and rigor. Her work has trained thousands of students and practitioners in a shared vocabulary and practical tools, while also serving as an on-ramp for a growing mainstream audience looking to engage astrology as a framework for self-understanding. Over decades, she has built a curriculum-driven ecosystem rooted in accountability, and her teaching has become a primary source of institutional knowledge in a field often dominated by shorthand. Silverman has also made her mark as a published author. Her first book, The Missing Element: Inspiring Compassion for the Human Condition (Findhorn Press), introduced her Four Elements framework to readers looking for language around temperament, patterns, and the parts of themselves they tend to judge, and it was later selected for Aaron Rodgers’ book club in 2022. Her second book, I Don’t Believe in Astrology: A Therapist’s Guide to the Life-Changing Wisdom of the Stars (St. Martin’s Essentials, April 2025), begins with a skeptic’s premise and builds a therapist’s argument, treating the chart as a practical framework for self-observation and accountability rather than a matter of belief. Debra’s influence extends well beyond her school. Across platforms, she has built a large, highly engaged audience of adult learners, particularly women, who return to her work for language around temperament, relationships, and the patterns that repeat until someone finally names them. She also hosts The I Don’t Believe in Astrology Podcast , a natural extension of her teaching, where she breaks down her framework in real time, defines terms with precision, and translates the chart into behavior you can recognize in yourself and in the people closest to you. That combination of institutional teaching and public-facing explanation has placed Silverman in a rare position: both a leading trainer within the field and a trusted interpreter for the broader culture. She has been sought out by public figures and creatives across industries; notable supporters and collaborators include Zach Bush, Gino Wickman, Aaron Rodgers, Sting, Tommy Chong, Jennifer Aniston, Julianne Hough, and India Arie. Taken together, her books, education platform, trainings, retreats, and media work operate as a cohesive body of instruction, with a shared vocabulary that students return to and practitioners carry forward. ee6dd2f0-7fde-4dbd-b3c6-23da56a2cb27: October Theme: “Broadway and Show Tunes” There’s nothing that brings people together better than singing our favorite songs. It recalls summer nights around the campfire: someone strumming the guitar and all singing a mix of folk music, familiar songs we heard on the radio, and occasional new songs that someone shares. Nobody has to worry about whether you know the songs or can sing like a pro. This is our chance to share the joy of singing simply for the fun of it. Cary Sheldon is a singer, songwriter, and beloved Berkeley voice teacher with 30 years worth of grateful students. She has been playing and teaching in the Bay Area for the last 40 years. Her love for R & B music led her to be part of Zazu Pitts Memorial Orchestra in the 1980’s. Other affiliations include The Henry Kaiser Band, The Henriettas (a recreation of DeZurick sisters, a popular country music duo from the 1940’s), who appeared on Prairie Home Companion, and most recently her band DanceChant, a joyful community-inspired R&B band that encourages audience participation. She continues to be inspired by her love of singing in community. “Singing together with others is one of the greatest joys in my life.” Now in her 60’s, she returns to influences from her early life. Her grade school music teachers included John Langstaff, creator of the Christmas Revels, and the repertoire was based on the American folk tradition, including old English ballads, spirituals, freedom songs, and the popular folk and protest songs of the 1960’s. She hopes to inspire others to explore the depth of this material and rediscover the joy of community singing. Soprano Candace Johnson has led AMN’s Juneteenth Choral Celebration since its inception in 2020. The AMN community knows her through her commitment to the power of the Negro Spirituals tradition, but Candace has a deep connection to theater and to the music of the Broadway stage. A voice instructor at UC Berkeley for 17 years, in 2022 Candace also became the director of the University Gospel Choir. A lyric coloratura soprano, she crosses musical boundaries performing classical, jazz, musical theater, pop and gospel. She has sung on many stages, including Carnegie Hall and The Manhattan Center. Also a playwright and actress, Candace premiered her first one-woman show, Vox in a Box , in UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall in 2018, which led to her becoming a resident solo artist at The Marsh theater (Berkeley/San Francisco). Candace has written and performed 5 full-length one-woman musicals. Her most recent show, Scat-ter Brain: The Music of ADHD , was commissioned by The Marsh in 2024 for its inaugural IFOYE festival of new works by women-identifying playwrights. Following an extended run, Scat-ter Brain was nominated by Broadway World SF for Best Solo Show of 2025. Please read our Health, Safety and COVID-19 Information Our commitment to our patrons

dfb53c1c-c28d-484e-af4f-4923131d2f25: What would you give for a chance to be the most omnipotent version of yourself? To finally be rid of the petty human desires that keep you from achieving greatness? To finally have it all, everything you’ve ever wanted? What would you trade? What are you willing to lose? What would you do for power? These questions are at the core of KiNG MALA’s debut album, And You Who Drowned In The Grief Of A Golden Thing . Across its wide-ranging 12 tracks – which seesaw between invigorating industrial pop and delicately refined R&B balladry – the singer-songwriter spins a tale as equally rooted in a sci-fi nightmare as it is in reality. The album follows the classic storyline of a hero’s journey to redemption, focusing on two non-descript, fictionalized characters: a human and an all-mighty entity. The front half is packed with the wonder of “what if.” What would an exchange for power look like? And more importantly, what would it sound like? (Think the experimental, living aesthetic of Bon Iver’s 22, A Million or Dijon's Absolutely , she offers – but with more bite.) The back half of the project provides answers – and it’s not pretty. By the story’s end, the human not only lacks power, but everything that made then human as well. “It's what we become, because the real dark shit that happens to women, you are never the same,” KiNG Mala shares. And at a time when the world is embracing such left-of-center storytelling, KiNG MALA is primed to emerge at the forefront of dark-pop’s new wave. “Everyone's being weird as fuck right now,” she says, citing world-building artists like Charli xcx and Chappell Roan and movies like The Substance . “We're moving into this space where we can be fucking freaks and finally be angry and disgusting – it's all manifesting.”
ff0d85a5-191a-4173-bf90-e44a666b31c9: Featuring Nate’ THESOULSANGER & Mirraje · Two powerful women. Two distinctive voices. One soulful night of music. NATE’ THESOULSANGER Some artists find their voice. Nate’ THESOULSANGER inherited hers. Born and raised in Oakland, Nate’ comes from a rich musical heritage as a descendant of the Grammy-winning Gospel Hummingbirds . Raised in a legacy of faith, storytelling, and soul, music was never simply something she discovered it was part of her foundation. An award-winning vocalist, international recording artist, songwriter, producer, actress, event host, and co-founder of SoulGlo Productions, LLC , THESOULSANGER has built a career that refuses to be confined to one genre. Her sound moves through soul, gospel, R&B, hip hop, theater, and beyond , bringing authenticity, power, and unmistakable Oakland soul to every performance. Throughout her career, she has shared stages and studios with artists including Patti LaBelle, Kelly Price, Carlos Santana, MC Hammer, LaRussell , and Grammy-winning producer Narada Michael Walden , with whom she has developed a longstanding creative relationship. Her voice is also woven into Bay Area music history. Nate’ created and recorded the memorable hook for Mac Dre’s “Make You Mine,” a song that became part of his enduring musical legacy. Her credits span radio, film, theater, live production, and recording. A Bay Area Rising Star and Best Vocalist award recipient , she has received KMEL airplay, contributed vocals to the Warner Bros. film The Invasion , and established herself as a trusted creative force both onstage and behind the scenes. At Yoshi’s Oakland , Nate’ has become such a familiar presence as a headliner, host, featured vocalist, producer, and collaborator that she earned the affectionate nickname “Ms. Yoshi’s.” Whether singing, producing, acting, hosting, mentoring, or creating opportunities for others, Nate’ brings the same qualities to every room: authenticity, excellence, soul, and connection. Singer. Songwriter. Producer. Actress. Host. Mentor. Community Builder. Oakland soul in every room she enters. Nate’ THESOULSANGER. The THE is intentional. CHRISTIE “MIRRAJE” MALONE Christie “Mirraje” Malone was born to sing. The daughter of blues musician George “Bluestone” Malone , Mirraje began singing at the age of three and writing songs and poetry by age nine. A gifted singer, songwriter, and natural stage performer, music has been woven into her life from the very beginning. Growing up in Los Angeles, Mirraje’s journey has been shaped by love, loss, perseverance, and an unwavering desire to create. After caring for her mother and experiencing her passing, Mirraje stepped away from singing and writing for four years. The memory of her mother—her greatest inspiration, biggest fan, and loudest cheerleader—eventually reignited her passion and gave her the courage to dream and create again. As she embarked upon her solo career, Mirraje recognized the extraordinary musical journey that had already taken shape. She has shared the stage with celebrated artists including Stevie Wonder, Evelyn “Champagne” King, Morris Day, Zapp, Club Nouveau, Cameo, Sugar Hill Gang, and Klymaxx . Mirraje’s musical influences span genres and generations, with Anita Baker holding a special place among her favorites. Her eclectic love of music allows her to find inspiration in the experiences, thoughts, emotions, and sounds that surround her. Rather than allowing her artistry to be defined by a particular genre or category, Mirraje creates from a place of freedom and authenticity. In her own words: “Life is unpredictable and unique. It should never be defined by genres or categories; nor should our music be. I just do what feels good.” SANG SIS! Together, Nate’ THESOULSANGER and Christie “Mirraje” Malone bring two extraordinary musical journeys to one stage for SANG SIS! —a celebration of powerful women, authentic voices, soulful storytelling, and music that refuses to be put in a box. Rooted in different musical legacies but connected by soul, these two women bring experience, grit, passion, and undeniable vocals to Yoshi’s Oakland for a night designed to make you feel something.

0977c4ba-c941-4ffa-8ec2-1bdfd1b0aa2f: In this deeply experiential yoga practice, we will explore the dynamic interplay between stability and mobility, strength and relaxation, movement and stillness. Through mindful movement, standing and seated practices, breath, and attention to the subtle ways we organize ourselves in space, we'll investigate what allows us to feel both grounded and free. This event happens each week at the Alembic. Rather than striving for perfect alignment or mastering difficult poses, we'll approach the practice as an exploration. We'll slow down enough to notice, experiment with different possibilities, and discover how the balance between effort and ease can change our experience of movement — and of ourselves.. Teacher Bio: Vickie Russell Bell has been teaching yoga for more than 30 years, bringing together the precision of alignment-based yoga with a deep curiosity about how we inhabit our bodies, regulate our nervous systems, and move through the world. She is an E-RYT 500 and Certified Yoga Therapist (C-IAYT), and has studied with some of the most respected teachers in the Iyengar-influenced yoga tradition. Her teaching is grounded in the belief that yoga is less about mastering poses than developing a more intimate relationship with ourselves. Her classes invite students to slow down, pay attention, and explore the constantly shifting relationships between stability and mobility, strength and softness, effort and ease. She teaches students of all ages and abilities, with a particular interest in yoga as a practice for living fully and well over time.
97ab2273-2503-4b4f-8a8f-301e6bd37840: Every Tuesday morning, the Alembic opens for a half-day of silent meditation practice. This is an unguided silent retreat consisting of three 40-minute meditation periods. There will be no teacher-led instruction during the meditation periods. Participants are invited to bring and engage in their own silent meditation practice. Whether you practice mindfulness, Zen, Vipassana, contemplation, prayer, or another silent form of meditation, all are welcome. The retreat begins promptly at 9:30 AM and concludes at 11:50 AM. Please arrive between 9:15 AM and 9:25 AM to remove your shoes, settle in, and find a seat before the first bell. The morning is divided into three periods of silent meditation: 9:30 AM – 10:10 AM 10:20 AM – 11:00 AM 11:10 AM – 11:50 AM A bell will signal the beginning and end of each meditation period. The meditation hall (Sol) is reserved for silent practice during sitting periods. Between sits, participants may quietly stretch, visit the restroom, or spend time in the tearoom. Conversation is permitted during breaks; however, we encourage participants to keep voices low, as some attendees choose to observe silence throughout the entire morning. You are welcome to leave the meditation hall at any time if needed. If you leave during a meditation period, please wait until the next break before re-entering. We ask that all entrances and exits be as quiet and unobtrusive as possible. This is a “Bring Your Own Silent Meditation” retreat. We provide the structure and the space; you provide your own silent practice. Participants may choose to sit in Sol or engage in quiet movement practice in the tearoom during meditation periods. To minimize disruption, please enter Sol only during the transition periods between sits. If you arrive after a meditation period has begun, you are welcome to practice elsewhere in the Alembic until the next bell. The suggested donation is $10. No one will be turned away for lack of funds. We do ask that all attendees register through the Momence app or via the registration link on the Alembic website. Please note that the retreat ends at 11:50 AM, and we ask all participants to depart by 12:00 PM so that our volunteer teacher and staff may close the space in a timely manner. Thank you for helping us maintain a quiet and supportive environment for practice.
cbfac66b-b293-49c9-bc8b-34329d869679: @ About Event Details Program PANELISTS & PERFORMERS Gallery Plan Your Visit Reserve Space Points Of Departure Fall 2026 Presented by Fort Mason Art Points Of Departure is a new series of immersive live events celebrating the spectrum of Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture (FMCAC) as a place for innovation and discovery, a personal port of embarkation for its community, and a window on the world. Each program celebrates the vibrant past, present, and future of FMCAC as it charts a course toward its 50th anniversary in 2027. Points Of Departure is curated by Brad Rosenstein, Associate Curator of Public Programs. Two Points Of Departure Fall 2026 Events Happen in The Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor Program 2 CIRCUS BY THE BAY Panel conversation and live performances Tuesday, October 13, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Cowell Theater, Pier 2/Gateway Pavilion, FMCAC , RESERVE SPACE Pickle Family Circus at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture Lively Arts Festival 1978. Photo: Terry Lorant In the 1970s, San Francisco became an epicenter of the emerging new American circus – an intimate one-ring model that spurned animal acts and focused on traditional skills of juggling, clowning, acrobatics, and aerial work, all filtered through a countercultural vaudevillian sensibility. This “not-so-big-top” was pioneered by such local companies as the Pickle Family Circus and its later incarnation, the New Pickle Circus, which performed annually at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture, and longtime FMCAC residents Make*A*Circus. This movement spawned a stream of Bay Area talents that spread their influence from Cirque du Soleil and Broadway to movies, and TV, an impact which resonates to this day. Join us for a magical evening celebrating this uniquely San Francisco history through a conversation with some of its leading lights, all veterans of Pickle Family Circus and the New Pickle Circus: performer/writer/director Gypsy Snider , trapeze artist/choreographer/director Shana Carroll , clown/writer/teacher Jeff Raz , and artistic director/choreographer Tandy Beal . The program includes rare archival photos and video, and live performances by Unique Derique ( Prescott Circus ), Chloe Somers Walier ( Dear San Francisco ), Elise Hing ( Circus Bella ), and performers from San Francisco Youth Circus ( SFYC ), Circus Center ’s pre-professional youth program. SFYC is led by Performance Coach Dominic Cruz , a 7 Fingers/ Dear San Francisco alum. (performers subject to change). Program 3 LIFE ON THE WATER: A REUNION Panel conversation and rare performance video Thursday, November 12, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor, Fort Mason Center or Arts & Culture , RESERVE SPACE LEFT TO RIGHT: LIFE ON THE WATER’s Bill Talen , Ellen Sebastian , Leonard Pitt , and Joe Lambert with a model of the Bayfront Theatre remodel 1987. LIFE ON THE WATER (LOTW) was an extraordinary presenting and producing organization based at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture for seven seasons between 1986-1993. Centered in its own custom-designed space (now the Bayfront Theatre), the company was dedicated to presenting artists who originated their own work and committed to a blend of experimental and traditional stage forms, political statement, and cultural diversity. It became nationally renowned for its pioneering showcases of solo theater work by such luminaries as Spalding Gray and Karen Finley as well as co-producing the annual Solo Mio Festival. LOTW’s presentations also ranged from music, dance, screenings, and workshops to ongoing programs such as Latino Theatre Project, Earth Drama Lab, and AsianImprov aRts (AIR). This special evening reunites LOTW’s founding directors Ellen Sebastian Chang , Bill Talen , Leonard Pitt , and Joe Lambert on their former stage for a sparkling conversation about the company’s groundbreaking work, which includes their own creations ranging from Pitt’s “avant mime” theater Not for Real and Sebastian’s epic The Sanctified Church to Talen’s biting satires such as Political Wife . The program includes never-before-seen archival video of some of LOTW’s most celebrated productions. Past Programs Program 1 TELL THEM WE WERE HERE Film screening and panel conversation Thursday, September 24, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor, Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture (FMCAC) , RESERVE SPACE TELL THEM WE WERE HERE Artist Alicia McCarthy Tell Them We Were Here (2021), a film by Griff Williams and Keelan Williams , chronicles visual/multidisciplinary artists currently living and working in the San Francisco Bay Area and how they extend the historical legacy of Bay Area creativity, activism, and community. Reflecting the spirit of FMCAC and its vibrant connection to local art and artists, the film centers the idea of art as a reflection of the place from which it emerges and helps to define the unique character of the Bay Area scene over the past 25 years. The film follows the work of Sadie Barnette , Amy Franceschini ( Futurefarmers ), Jim Goldberg , Tucker Nichols , Lynn Hershman Leeson , Alicia McCarthy , Nigel Poor ( Ear Hustle ), and M ichael Swaine , a select group of artists who have chosen a less-worn path. It touches on the disappearance of cultural communities due to gentrification and economic instability, while reminding us of art’s power to transform and how vital creative communities are to healthy societies and political change. The screening is followed by a panel discussion with director Griff Williams , artists Amy Franceschini and Tucker Nichols , and curator René de Guzman (all featured in the film), exploring how the local art scene has continued to evolve in the five years since the film’s premiere. All Fort Mason Art programs are generously supported by San Francisco Grants for The Arts, the FMCAC Board of Directors, and individual contributions to the Fort Mason Fund. PANELISTS & PERFORMERS PANELISTS TELL THEM WE WERE HERE : Griff Williams is an American painter, publisher and gallerist. In 1993 he founded Gallery 16 and the pioneering fine art printmaking workshop Urban Digital Color in San Francisco. The exhibition and publishing program has worked with hundreds of artists including Lynn Hershman Leeson, William Kentridge, Deborah Oropallo, Jim Isermann, bell hooks, Rex Ray, Margaret Kilgallen, Mark Grotjahn, Paul Sietsema, Arturo Herrera, Michelle Grabner, and Ari Marcopoulos. Williams has also designed and published dozens of acclaimed books with the Gallery 16 Editions imprint. His paintings have been exhibited in galleries and museums including the San Diego Museum of Art, the Crocker Art Museum in Sacramento, and the San Jose Museum of Art . His work has been reviewed in Art in America , Flash Art , and ARTnews . He co-directed Tell Them We Were Here with his son, Keelan Williams , a filmmaker based in Los Angeles. René de Guzman is a longtime Bay Area curator, artist, and arts consultant. He was one of the founding curators at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts as Visual Arts Curator and Director of Visual Arts, serving from 1993-2007, and subsequently served as the Senior Curator of Art and Director of Exhibition Strategy at the Oakland Museum of California from 2007-21. He also served as Deputy Director for Programs and Engagement at Headlands Center for the Arts , overseeing artist residencies and public programs. For more than three decades, he has developed innovative and popular exhibitions for a wide public and is currently Co-Director of Art + Water in San Francisco. Amy Franceschini is an artist whose work facilitates encounter, exchange, and tactile forms of inquiry by calling into question the “certainties” of a given time or place where a work is situated. In 1995, Franceschini founded Futurefarmers as a collaborative platform to consider the social, political, and environmental organization of space. Futurefarmers use various media to deconstruct systems to visualize and understand their intrinsic logics; food systems, public transportation, education … Through this disassembly they find new narratives and reconfigurations that form alternatives to the principles that once dominated these systems. Franceschini received her BFA in Photography from San Francisco State University and an MFA from Stanford University. She has taught in the visual arts graduate programs at California College of the Arts in San Francisco and Stanford University and in the Master of Eco-Social Design at the Free University in Bolzano, Italy. She is a 2009 Guggenheim Fellow, a 2019 Rome Prize Fellow and a 2017 recipient of the Herb Alpert Award for Visual Arts. Tucker Nichols is an artist based in Northern California. His work has been featured at the Drawing Center in New York, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the Denver Art Museum, Den Frie Museum in Copenhagen, and the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. A show of his sculpture, Almost Everything On The Table , was recently on view at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum. His drawings have been published in McSweeney’s , The Thing Quarterly , The New Yorker , and the Op-Ed pages of The New York Times . He is co-author of the books, Crabtree (with Jon Nichols) and This Bridge Will Not Be Gray (with Dave Eggers). Flowers for Sick People , his ongoing multimedia project, was featured on the PBS Newshour and the subject of an exhibition at SFMOMA, Close to Home: Creativity in Crisis , is an exhibition highlighting seven local artists’ responses to the pandemic. He is represented by ZieherSmith in New York and Gallery 16 in San Francisco. CIRCUS BY THE BAY : Gypsy Snider is co-artistic director of Dear San Francisco , now celebrating its fifth anniversary at the city’s historic Club Fugazi. As co-founding artistic director of The 7 Fingers , she wrote and directed SisterS , Réversible, Intersection , Amuse , Un D i a , Traces , and Loft . She has choreographed televised feature performances for America’s Got Talent and Her Majesty’s Royal Variety Performance . In 2013, working with director Diane Paulus on a new vision of Pippin , she created choreography and wove circus into the revival of the Broadway musical, earning her a Drama Desk Award and an Outer Critics Circle Award. Snider began her circus career at the age of four when her parents founded The Pickle Family Circus. She grew up touring the West Coast with the company. In 2002, while in her hometown of San Francisco, she wrote and directed for The New Pickle Circus a show entitled Circumstance , which premiered at FMCAC’s Cowell Theater. Snider is also a guest teacher and guest director at the National Circus School of Montreal. Shana Carroll is co-artistic director of Dear San Francisco , and co-founding artistic director of The 7 Fingers . Since the latter’s inception in 2002, Shana has directed, written, and created choreography for a dozen or so of their touring and/or resident shows, including Passagers , Cuisine & Confessions , Séquence 8 , and Traces . in 2024 Carroll was co-choreographer and Circus Designer for Water For Elephants on Broadway, for which she received the Chita Rivera Award for Best Choreography, as well as Tony, Drama Desk, and Outer Critics Circles nominations in the same category. Carroll has frequently collaborated with Cirque du Soleil , most recently as co-director of their first show on ice, Crystal , and previously as acrobatic designer and choreographer of Paramour (Broadway) and Iris (Los Angeles), and as director/choreographer of their performance at the 2012 Academy Awards. Originally from Berkeley, CA, and daughter of beloved San Francisco columnist Jon Carroll, Shana began her career as a trapeze artist with San Francisco’s Pickle Family Circus and went on to a 20-year career in the air with Cirque du Soleil and many others before co-founding The 7 Fingers. Jeff Raz has performed nationally and internationally for decades, starring in the Pickle Family Circus, Cirque du Soleil’s Corteo , Make*A*Circus, and many other circuses and theaters. Jeff is also a playwright, director, teacher, producer and has authored four books inspired by his career. Over the years he has also co-founded six arts organizations and worked globally as a communications and leadership consultant. Tandy Beal is a performer, director, choreographer, writer, teacher, and … dreamer. An off-the-map career includes: directing Pickle Family Circus for 10 years; touring four continents with Tandy Beal & Co.; writing/directing VIVA for the Moscow Circus in Japan; a show for NASA’s SETI project with Carl Sagan; projects with Lou Harrison, Frank Zappa, John Adams, and decades of projects with Bobby McFerrin, Art Lande, and Jon Scoville; choreographing opera, MTV, ballet; corporate shows (LucasFilms, SF 49ers, MCI, Coca-Cola, Pixar, Oracle+); acting off-Broadway; dancing for the Shah of Iran with Alwin Nikolais in Tehran; guest performances with Atlanta Ballet, Momix, Remy Charlip and in Europe, with Carolyn Carlson; creating what Dance Magazine said was the first contemporary dance/circus Nutcracker . Her life and work are featured in two books, The Pickle Clowns and Living Happily Ever After . She has received awards from AFI, CAC, NEA, Packard, and Hewlett +. Her natural habitat is the Santa Cruz mountains where she lives with longtime co-conspirator, Jon Scoville. PANELISTS LIFE ON THE WATER: A REUNION : Ellen Sebastian Chang is a distinguished multidisciplinary director, dramaturge, writer, and arts educator with a career spanning 50 years, dedicated to advocating for human rights and understanding through the creative arts. She has collaborated with a diverse array of artists and art forms: theater, opera, dance, radio, film and installation. Sebastian Chang commenced her career as a lighting technician and designer before making her debut as a director and writer in 1982 with Your Place Is No Longer With Us , an immersive play staged in private homes about a biracial girl. She co-founded LIFE ON THE WATER (LOTW), a notable producing organization in San Francisco, and served as its co-artistic director. During her time at LOTW she created The Sanctified Church with Luisah Teisch, later renamed Sanctified with Esther Scott, No Trace of the Blonde with Holly Hughes, and Janie Geiser, FACE with Bob Ernst, Artis Fountaine, NAO, and Debora Iyall. She has been the creative director and teaching artist for The World As It Could Be Human Rights Education Program, utilizing the arts to deepen understanding of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and inspire activism across generations. Beyond her work in theater, she co-owned the award-winning FuseBOX restaurant in West Oakland created with Chef Sunhui Chang. She has received numerous grants and fellowships from prestigious arts foundations such as Creative Capital, Kenneth Rainin Foundation, MAP Fund, National Endowment for the Arts, and Ruth Arts Fellowship. Her current focus is rewilding six acres of land in the Pacific Northwest planting 1,350 native trees with foresters Boots on the Ground. William Talen grew up in small towns throughout Minnesota, South Dakota, and Wisconsin, and came west in the 70s, joining the poetry community in Bolinas, CA before moving to North Beach. Exploring storytelling techniques with solo shows in the Eureka Theater and Intersection, he studied with Spalding Gray and Sidney Lanier. Talen then partnered with Ellen Sebastian, and in 1984 they dreamed of a radical kind of theater, inspired by the stage sets of restaurants and the parties of Anon Salon, eventually lifting “Life on the Water” from a billboard in front of a yuppie apartment complex in Richmond, CA. Gathering with Joe Lambert and Leonard Pitt, LOTW kicked off with six weeks of Gray in the fall of ’86. After seven years, Talen departed for New York, leaving the Solo Mio Festival to Marcia Crosby, Joegh Bullock, and Kate Boyd. In New York and Europe, his character “Reverend Billy” caught a wave of post-religious spiritual hunger, inventing the movement against Consumerism by the time of 9/11. With director and life partner Savitri D, daughter Lena Nightstar, and a revolving troupe of 30 singers, the “Church of Stop Shopping” staged earth services at a series of NYC “art churches” and toured shows on five continents, always returning to justice campaigns in New York. In 2016, Neil Young and Daryl Hannah proposed that Talen preach his “Earthalujah” gospel at the opening of each show, which kicked off a 10-year collaboration, performing in 35 amphitheaters and reaching about 650,000 in Young’s rock audiences. Currently, the Stop Shopping Church has settled in the 500-seat Quaker Meetinghouse in Manhattan, the anti-consumerism of its early days now centered on the Earth’s crisis. Talen’s books include The Earth Wants You from City Lights, and now his fifth book, Earthalujah! , being published in November by Autonomedia Press. Leonard Pitt studied mime in Paris with Etienne Decroux for four years, becoming his assistant and performing in his company. On his return to the U.S., Pitt settled in Berkeley, CA, where he opened a school of physical theater, attracting students from around the world. Pitt’s one-man shows have received critical acclaim. He has performed and taught at theaters and festivals throughout the U.S., Europe, Brazil, New Zealand, and Australia. He was also a member of George Coates Performance Works and traveled widely with the company. In Bali he studied mask theatre and performed extensively with his teacher. In 1986, he co-founded LOTW, where his projects included the “avant-mime” production Not for Real (created with Rinde Eckert), Spleenix , The Art of Face , and performing David Barth’s solo play, Ned . In 1991, Leonard created Eco-Rap, an environmental education program combining ecology and rap music as a way to educate inner city youth about urgent social issues. He has written and published seven books, including three books on Paris and a memoir, and created numerous videos on Paris, all viewable on YouTube ( Leonard Pitt Paris ). He continues to live in Berkeley and create and is currently working on two new books. Joe Lambert is the founder of StoryCenter and the originator of the digital storytelling movement, a participatory media methodology used by 100,000s of people all over the world. The work has taken him and his organization to all 50 U.S. states, and more than 90 countries. Earlier in his career, he served as Executive Director of the People’s Theater Coalition and LOTW, where he executive-produced more than 500 performances, festivals, conferences, and national gatherings. Highlights include the first San Francisco Jazz Tap Festival, collaborations with artists like Guillermo Gomez Peña, the Blue Man Group, Marty Pottenger, and Dana Atchley. During that time, he held leadership roles in national initiatives including the Alliance for Cultural Democracy and the National Performance Network, and served as a panelist and principal consultant for numerous public agencies and private foundations. As an author and curriculum developer, he has written numerous articles. For projToday, based in Santa Fe, NM, he continues this work through StoryHost LLC, teaching workshops, hosting the Elderware podcast, and exploring the intersections of story, aging, and meaning-making. PERFORMERS CIRCUS BY THE BAY : Unique Derique , an internationally acclaimed entertainer, is a cornerstone of the Bay Area circus and performing arts scene. He honed his physical comedy with premier troupes including Circus A La Mode, Make*A*Circus, and the historic Pickle Family Circus. Dedicated to community arts education, Derique has spent nearly three decades as an Artist-in Residence at West Oakland’s Prescott Circus Theater, teaching youth the art and history of Hambone body percussion. His versatile talent has graced international television and stages worldwide, opening for legends like Lou Rawls, Sammy Davis Jr., and The Temptations. Annually, his holiday show Fool La La: Whimsical brings joy to all ages at The Marsh Berkeley. Elise Hing , born and raised in Santa Cruz, CA, discovered her natural flexibility at age 12 and quickly developed a passion for contortion. For the past five years she has performed with Circus Bella doing free shows in the park during the summer and under the big top in the winter for their holiday spectacular. She has also appeared with Flynn Creek Circus and continues to gig all over the bay area. Hing loves to connect and delight audiences through her playful, awe-inspiring shapes and movements but outside of the ring she enjoys being out in nature with friends and pursuing creative projects like sewing. Chloe Somers Walier , known as the “Megawatt Smile,” is an effervescent circus performer with eight years of international touring experience with Les 7 Doigts de la main, performing in Passengers , Duel Reality , and Dear San Francisco . A multidisciplinary performer specializing in hula hoop, trapeze, group acrobatics, and bottle walking – balancing in heels on top of wine bottles – she has performed at three international circus festivals and received the People’s Choice Award from Riga Cirks. With a love for the unexpected and a playful spirit at the heart of her work, she brings a warm, joyful energy to the stage, blending technical skill and theatricality with a little bit of sparkle and a lot of personality. San Francisco Youth Circus (SFYC) performers are part of Circus Center’s pre-professional youth program. 2514af8f-1dc2-48f9-831e-4b8bc6e067e1: Packages is a novel about the stories we tell to survive—and the ones that haunt us when survival isn’t enough. At once tender and unsettling, Packages announces a bold new literary voice and marks the arrival of a writer unafraid to look directly at the cost of looking away. Set against the charged intimacy of a Southern college town, Danny O’Dea’s debut follows Michael McKnight, a young man orbiting grief, desire, and moral uncertainty as he navigates friendship, sexuality, faith, and the quiet violence of complicity. When a series of mysterious packages begin arriving at an off-campus house, Michael finds himself drawn into a web of secrecy that forces him to confront not only what his peers are capable of, but what he himself is willing to ignore. Moving fluidly between memory and present action, Packages is both a coming-of-age story and a reckoning—about masculinity, queerness, guilt, and the ways institutions and friendships fail the most vulnerable. With prose that is sharp, intimate, and darkly funny, O’Dea captures the intoxicating freedom of youth alongside its moral blind spots, asking how responsibility is formed, deferred, or abandoned altogether. 6e1a5914-62f6-44bd-9ab0-57407fafff76: The revolution had a sex life. · The late 1960s told young women to get free—sexually, politically, artistically. And for many, those freedoms were exhilarating. But liberation could also create contradictions of its own. In Alexis Krasilovsky’s new novel, Portrait of an Artist as a Young Woman , an aspiring filmmaker plunges into the art and sexual experimentation of the era, navigating desire, ambition, creative possibility, exploitation, and old hierarchies in new clothes. Judy Juanita’s Virgin Soul , meanwhile, follows a young Black woman drawn into the revolutionary politics of the Black Panther Party, where idealism, danger, race, sex, and power collide. Krasilovsky and Juanita—whose own lives intersect with the histories their novels revisit—come together at Clio’s to interrogate the mythology of liberation from the inside. What did “free love” offer women, and what did it demand of them? Could radical movements escape the inequalities of the society they wanted to overthrow? And what did it take for a woman to insist on being not someone’s muse, girlfriend, comrade, or supporting character, but an artist and political actor in her own right? Moving between fiction and lived history, from the New York art world and the emergence of women filmmakers to the Black Panthers and Oakland, their conversation asks what happens when women tell the story of a supposedly liberated generation for themselves. Alexis Krasilovsky is an award-winning filmmaker, author, and Professor Emerita of Cinema and Television Arts at California State University, Northridge. A member of Yale’s first coeducational graduating class, she made End of the Art World , featuring Andy Warhol, Robert Rauschenberg, Jasper Johns, Roy Lichtenstein, and other major artists. Her decades-long work on women and filmmaking includes the documentary Women Behind the Camera and the books Women Behind the Camera: Conversations with Camerawomen and Shooting Women: Behind the Camera, Around the World . Her new novel, Portrait of an Artist as a Young Woman , will be published by City Point Press in September 2026. Judy Juanita is an award-winning poet, novelist, playwright, and essayist whose work spans race, gender, radical politics, and California life. Her semi-autobiographical novel Virgin Soul follows a young Black woman drawn into the Black Panther Party in the late 1960s. Her recent books include the memoir California Fever Dream and Abortion (or Woman as Threefold Murderess) . Her poetry collection Manhattan my ass, you’re in Oakland won the 2021 American Book Award from the Before Columbus Foundation, and her essay collection DeFacto Feminism: Essays Straight Outta Oakland examines race, gender, politics, and spirituality through the perspective of a Black activist and self-described “feminist foot soldier.”

8c6a282c-bfe2-469d-bdbb-53bab386bc25: Join Yotam Ottolenghi for an intimate and energizing evening celebrating his forthcoming Fall 2026 cookbook, Simple Too , the long-awaited follow-up to his bestselling Ottolenghi Simple. In conversation, he’ll share how Simple Too was born from real life: recipes that work with you, not against you — dishes you can begin with half a plan and still end with a deeply satisfying meal. Drawing from the book’s vibrant themes, Ottolenghi will dive into the ingredients and techniques that quietly shape this new collection: beans simply dressed, black chickpeas, sesame in generous handfuls, sweet- and-spicy balances, pasta cooked directly in its sauce, and whole meals roasted start-to-finish in a single tray (with far less washing up). Through stories from the writing process with co-author Verena Lochmuller, practical tips, and reflections on finding pleasure in cooking even when you’re already tired, Ottolenghi will reveal how SIMPLE TOO is less about doing less — and more about making everyday cooking feel generous, achievable, and full of joy. f3e3362e-2294-457a-92ab-1c865c45024a: Sitting at the forefront of contemporary jazz · 'Well, at least nobody could ever accuse us of releasing too much music!’ quips GregCarmichael on the release of their latest EP “The Empire of Lights”, ‘but I think our fans know by now that we’re a little obsessive about only releasing music when we have something ready that we really love.’ The four tracks on their latest release visit familiar themes for longtime fans, from the western shuffle of “8,000 Miles” to the reggae flavours of “Alisio”, the upbeat joy of “Back to Back” to the laid back groove of “Other People”. ‘We hope there’s something here for everyone,” says Miles Gilderdale, “we’re very lucky that over the years we’ve found fans that just get what we’re doing, so we can wear our influences on our sleeves and not have to try and fit into any one style.’ With over 35 years of recording and touring, the band’s longevity may be due in part to that spirit of never trying to fit in, but to just making music that they love. ‘I feel really grateful that we’ve been on such a long journey with our fans and they’re still there with us.’ Greg says, ‘We talk after shows, and it’s always such an honor to hear the stories of how our music has been the soundtrack to so many people’s lives.’ This EP is the first of a series of shorter musical releases that will eventually combine into a full album.’ Miles says, ‘We know that these days people listen to our music in lots of different ways, but I think we all remember the thrill of bringing a new record home and listening from start to finish, so we try and make sure everything we release works in that way as well as on playlists.’ The Empire of Lights will be released to all music platforms worldwide on June 13th, 2025, and a limited run of CDs will be pressed to be available to purchase at live shows.

Here Faye has performed alchemy, turning the words on the page into gothic gold.” — Lisa Unger An orphaned young woman in antebellum Maryland is pulled into a maelstrom of passion, pain, and occult power in this Gothic homage to the life and works of Edgar Allan Poe. Raven Helen Alan has always been haunted by witchcraft. Since the death of her beloved mother, she has soothed herself by speaking words into spells—a proclivity enhanced by time spent with her aunt’s library of occult books. After an itinerant childhood, Raven is relieved to finally settle down with Aunt Berenice in her Baltimore townhouse. There she finds a long-sought sense of belonging with the family of enslaved workers in her aunt’s household, especially the brilliantly odd youngest daughter Pym. Raven’s infatuation with her friend only grows more intimate as the girls become women together. But when the household is threatened with financial ruin, Raven must set out to earn her own living. Taking a job as a paid companion, Raven arrives at the crumbling Moldavia Manor. Her charge is a delicate young invalid named Lenore Legrand who haunts the Gothic structure like a phantom. Living with them is Lenore’s devoted older cousin Travanion, who spends his days searching ancient texts for an Elixir of Life that might cure Lenore. Raven finds herself inexorably drawn to both cousins as well as the to secrets hidden in the shadows of Moldavia Manor. But those secrets may just be the death of her... “A literary high wire act—combining clever homage with creativity and passion, a celebration of all things Poe, and treasures galore for fans to discover. Raven is the new essential gothic—layered, compelling, witty and entirely entertaining.” —Hank Phillippi Ryan Lyndsay Faye is the internationally bestselling author of eight critically acclaimed novels and two short story collections. She has been published in fifteen languages, nominated for two Edgar Awards, and received an American Library Association award for Best Historical Novel. A notable writer of Sherlock Holmes pastiches including Dust and Shadow and Observations by Gaslight , she also particularly enjoys upending classical literature, as in Jane Steele , which transforms Jane Eyre into a feminist serial killer. A true New Yorker in the sense that she was born elsewhere, Faye lives in Queens with her husband Nicholas and her cat Prufrock. f504f699-769e-46d0-ae85-ab9bbc6dcbd6: How Trees Make Our World · Robert Macfarlane writes “There is no lone tree language, but a forest of tree languages.” In The Language of Trees , Katie Holten invites us to enter some of these forests. She created a Tree Alphabet to translate a compendium of well known, loved, lost and new writing. She takes readers on a journey from creation myths and cave paintings to the death of a 3,500 year-old cypress tree, from Tree Clocks in Mongolia and forest fragments in the Amazon to Emerson’s language of fossil poetry, unearthing a grove of beautiful stories along the way. Listening, speaking, reading and writing are how humans communicate and make sense of the world. The alphabet is how we organize information and knowledge; our networked world depends on it. Trees, the font, lets us renew our relationships with language, landscape, perception, time, memory and reading itself by slowing the reader down to decipher words in the woods. Katie Holten will be in conversation with writer and editor Marthine Satris to discuss our relationship with literature and landscape and the unexpected and imaginative language inspired by the beauty of the natural world. Katie Holten is an award-winning artist and environmental activist. Holten's work investigates the entangled relationships between humans and the natural world. At the root of her practice is a call for Rights of Nature and a commitment to fighting the climate and biodiversity emergency. Her collaborative research based work explores the inextricable relationship between organic systems and human-made systems. She has created Tree Alphabets , a Forest Alphabet , and a Wildflower Alphabet to share the joy she finds in her love of the more-than-human world. Her work has appeared in The New Yorker, The New York Times, Artforum, and The Guardian. She is a visiting lecturer at the New School of the Anthropocene. Katie Holten’s book The Language of Trees was published in 2023 and became an instant bestseller. Holten lives between New York City and Ireland. If she could be a tree, she would be an Oak. Marthine Satris is a writer and editor living in Oakland. She is the Associate Publisher at Heyday, the nonprofit press in Berkeley, where she edits books about California's history, culture, and natural world. Her own poetry and prose have been published in The Georgia Review, The San Francisco Chronicle, Antiphony Journal, Santa Clara Review, Ballast Journal , and elsewhere. She is a frequent contributor to Oakland Review of Books.

0f453208-5b8b-4992-a580-05db3e4fd0f8: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. He draws from a decade of experience guiding men’s circles, performance dance teams, applied AI research, and meditation. Some recent inspirations of his are Ego Development Theory, madhyamaka philosophy, and Brazilian zouk. He is known for his steady, compassionate presence and calibrated relational risk-taking. He works full-time at the intersection of mental health and AI as a machine learning researcher.

3fd127df-75d1-4215-928f-3ac41b5e71d0: The best-selling author of "Fed Up" shares her brave and intimate memoir which shows how women's anger can lead us towards change. Join us at Mrs. Dalloway's Bookstore on Wednesday, October 14 when best-selling author Gemma Hartley comes to the store to share her new memoir No One Loves an Angry Woman: An Exvangelical Coming-of-Rage Story. Gemma will be joined in conversation by Tracy Clark-Flory and will sign copies of her book after the presentation. “A seething read that burns to the bone.” —Tia Levings, New York Times best-selling author of A Well-Trained Wife Gemma Hartley grew up in an Evangelical household where she was raised to become an obedient wife from the time she was a little girl. A sexual assault as a teenager upended her evangelical world, and that coupled with an upbringing steeped in purity culture led her to internalize guilt, silence… and anger. The good girl conditioning of the church demanded that Hartley seek the narrow path of womanhood that emphasized service to others, to swallow the discomfort and rage that simmered just below the surface – but when political events reawakened her trauma, she began to come apart at the seams. Here she unravels the threads of her upbringing to weave a new story, one where women’s anger is not sinful and dangerous – it is information, and often the most rational response there is. Whether or not you’ve ever set foot in a church, Christian patriarchal norms have shaped American culture in ways that are far-reaching and insidious. From restrictive legislation that takes away women’s bodily autonomy to cultural norms that expect women to pick up after their husbands and joyfully give up their careers to care for children—these are all standards informed and fed by Christian culture. Tying together her Christian upbringing together with a feminist examination of society today, Hartley tells her personal story, but it’s bigger than that: No One Loves an Angry Woman is the story of a cultural awakening.

b379d588-3736-4c6b-9f31-f39aa6c0ad21: Formed in 2019, Anhad Naad Collective is a genre-defying ensemble rooted in the exploration of South Asian musical traditions and their intersections with global genres. The collective had its debut concert in 2020 in San Francisco, led by core members Divya Purohit Vyas and Jun Ishimuro (of Qb Moda Jazz). Initially, their work centered around blending South Asian raga-based music with the soulful textures of jazz, R&B, and Black musical traditions. With a flexible and evolving lineup of collaborating artists, Anhad Naad Collective has performed at notable Bay Area venues including Bird & Beckett, Integral Yoga Institute, the Golden Gate Park Bandstand, and events such as San Francisco’s Summer of Music hosted by Noise Pop. In 2023, the group expanded its focus to delve deeper into South Asian spiritual music, with a special emphasis on Sufi Qawwali traditions. Anhad Naad treats the spiritual dimension of Sufi poetry and music with deep reverence, often seeking guidance from poets and experts from Pakistan and India. Lead vocalist Divya Purohit Vyas has previously been a part of Bay Dervish in Alameda, a spiritual music collective associated with Sufi Way, led by the late Kiran Rana and Jeanne Rana. fe5f0e4d-88d4-4237-94c0-dfe88ebf112f: On the afternoon of his first appearance onstage with the Sex Pistols, last summer at Bush Hall, Frank Carter’s peaceful afternoon stroll on the streets of Shepherd’s Bush was interrupted by a stranger sat outside a pub. “Big shoes,” the man shouted; nothing more, nothing less. “That’s all he said,” Carter reports. “And I just replied ‘thanks for noticing’, and off I walked. But I thought, ‘Fucking hell, we’ve not even played one note yet’. At that point I felt like I was melting. I realised I had to get my shit together here.” As if the matter was ever in doubt, hours later, he did just that. The stranger’s assertion that anyone stepping up to the microphone with the band who terrorised a nation faces one of the tallest orders in rock and roll – make no mistake, filling big shoes requires big cojones – overlooked the fact that he was speaking to one of the few singers, and perhaps even the < Such was its success, in fact, that this short series of concerts has blossomed into a busy diary. This year, Carter and the Pistols – drummer Paul Cook, guitarist Steve Jones and bassist Glen Matlock – are set to perform in Australia, New Zealand, Japan, the United States of America, mainland Europe, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere. They’ll headline halls and appear at festivals. In March, the group will top the bill at a Teenage Cancer Trust concert at the Royal Albert Hall, of all places. Much more of this and they’ll be playing at Buckingham Palace. For anyone who might be wondering, they’re doing these things because, in 2025, the Pistols are sensational once more. And they’re doing it is because they want to. “What I live by now is, if it ain’t fun, I ain’t doing it,” the always reliably blunt Steve Jones says. “I’m too fucking old to be putting up with a bunch of old shit and acting like everything’s cool just to keep the ball rolling. Those days are gone. If it ain’t fun, honestly, I’m out of here. I ain’t got the energy for any crap any more.” The credit for bringing Frank Carter into the orbit of the Pistols belongs to Glen Matlock’s youngest son. As a member of the erstwhile group Dead!, Louis Matlock had seen the singer leading the charge while touring the UK as special guests to Frank Carter & The Rattlesnakes. Night after night, he witnessed the fearlessness of a performer who approached live music as if it were a collision sport. Big shoes be damned, if you’re looking for a singer, the son told the father, Frank’s your man. “Louis said, the guy you need is Frank Carter,” Glen Matlock says. “So I got his number off him and we arranged to have a coffee. I didn’t know much about him but Louis was always going on about him. So we had a play with him and Paul – Steve was out of the country – and Paul liked him, as did I, so we told Steve. I also went to see the Rattlesnakes at the Roundhouse [in Camden Town], where they did two sold out nights, and I was impressed. Then Steve came over [from his home in Los Angeles] and we started rehearsing and that was it.” Asked to nominate the exact point at which he realised that this new version of the Sex Pistols became a force to be reckoned with, Paul Cook replies that it was during the marching-boots style drum intro to Holidays In The Sun, the first song on the first night at Bush Hall. “As soon as we did Holidays… I thought, ‘Yeah, this is working,” he says. “This is going to be brilliant. This is going to be fantastic.” I was at the back there, looking at Frank with his red hair, and I was kind of getting flashbacks a little bit. I just thought, ‘Wow, this is how it was and how it should be’.” Naturally, Carter himself needed no introduction to the Sex Pistols. Raised in a home in the satellite town of Watford that groaned from the weight of vinyl LPs, as a 14-year-old, he would listen to his father’s copy of the epochal Never Mind The Bollocks… Here’s The Sex Pistols whenever his parents were out of the house. Smitten by its irresistible mix of fury and wit, blood and thunder, like countless other artists-to-be before him, he was at once captivated. Its guiding light helped lead him to the stage, and, in time, to < “The one thing I took from the album that I put immediately into the way I perform was just the energy of it,” Carter says. “I’ve heard records that < So, please, let us not be in any doubt as to his credentials as an MC of chaos. In 2008, 36 years after two members of the Pistols challenged each other to a fight after discovering they were playing different songs onstage at the 100 Club, at the same venue, as the singer with Gallows, Carter chased an audience member who had thrown a pint of lager onstage up the venue’s stairs and out onto Oxford Street < He even helped orchestrate his own Great Rock and Roll Swindle. In 2009, after Warner Bros. signed Gallows for a million quid, the group handed their new label the pummelling and furious Grey Britain, an album that seemed designed to repel the casual listener. “Britain is fucked,” Carter said at the time. “Grey Britain is all about what’s going on socially, politically and economically in the UK, and how it affects us.” Sound familiar? As in, there is no future in England’s dreaming? Of course, in 2025, bands and artists are less inclined than they once were to sing about issues that affect and bedevil an entire nation. With social media replacing punk rock as the fastest route into the public bloodstream, rock and roll has entered an introspective phase. Just as well, then, that the Pistols’ State of the Union Address remains as pressing, and as prescient, as ever. Inevitably, in the (almost) half century that has elapsed since a pair of Millwall supporting hot dog vendors in Piccadilly Circus unwittingly provided Steve Jones with the title for his group’s sole bona fide album – “never mind the bollocks,” they would say, meaning “don’t bother with that…” – London and Britain have changed almost beyond recognition. But at street level, the problems and frustrations remain the same. The Pistols themselves, though, < It’s different, too, because in 2025 the group’s personnel no longer comprises elements of soap opera, or pantomime. Instead, unity and teamwork are the makings of the new machine; the cohesion of drums, bass, guitar and voice in the service of the songs. In this iteration, the rock and roll itself is allowed to shine, timeless and evergreen. There is no swindle. The people who wrote and played the music back in ’76 and ’77 are able to enjoy it anew. “Don’t forget, the three of us learned to play together,” Glen Matlock says. “It was all pretty much at a similar level of competency when we started out. And we kind of grew together as musicians.” And now? “Put it this way,” he adds, “someone who is close to the band, I won’t say who, said it’s the first time they’ve seen us coming offstage with smiles on our faces since ’96. Which is good, because life’s too short for all that bollocks, really.” As for what might come after the Sex Pistols have said hello and goodnight to audiences across the globe, no one is saying because no one seems to know. The promise of new music that was extinguished by a television interview with Bill Grundy and the subsequent shellshock of a young band receiving too much of everything, far too soon for anyone, may never be realised. But who can say for sure? At least for now, there’s no point in asking - you’ll get no reply. But what we do have, for sure, is Frank Carter and the Sex Pistols whipping up a storm across the globe in a manner that is familiar but fresh, old but new. Catch it while you can, for as long as it lasts. Because we won’t see their kind again.

c9598cf0-ea7f-4d4f-a85b-d99b0987775b: Embodiment Practices is an invitation to practice giving ourselves permission to arrive fully to where we are, and gently explore movement and stillness to care for our bodies and ourselves. This event happens each week at the Alembic. As an element of self attunement, we will practice making intuitive choices through a lens of self love, meaning that we are each making choices that are nourishing and responsive to ourselves as individuals in that moment. Part of this practice includes being very intentional and explicit about what kinds of choices we might consider, and being curious about how it feels to try them. There will be many options provided throughout, with guidance around how to navigate choice making, including if this is new to you or you are navigating a limitation or injury. There will be a corner of the room set aside in case you’d like to opt out of the facilitated structure and take a moment for yourself to rest. Opening Circle: We'll ground and check-in with whatever feels present for each of us. We get to welcome ourselves to come as we are. Warm Up: We'll do a guided, full-bodied warm up, tuning the instruments of our bodies and attention, giving ourselves time to shake it out, stretch, wiggle, and move through whatever feels stuck. Movements will be simple enough to follow along, giving us a chance to get out of our heads and drop into our bodies, regulating our nervous system. Drawing on contemporary dance and yoga, there will be flow, rhythm, and music. Movement Explorations: We'll explore movements that deepen our connection with our bodies and our intuition, focusing on concepts and areas of the body that can help us settle and release. Meditation: Finally, we'll settle into meditation and rest. Finding stillness might be sitting/standing/lying down and might include cozy props, having eyes open or closed, and suggestions to make yourself comfortable, including allowing some body movement within that quiet space. Please bring clothes you feel comfortable to move in. It’s recommended to bring long sleeves, long pants and socks with you, in case we are moving on the floor. Bring a journal if you’d like. About Suzanne (Zan): With three decades of contemporary/modern dance experience and 15 years of teaching, Suzanne Beahrs guides students in exploring movement as a pathway to deeper connection—with ourselves, our surroundings, and each other. Her classes blend technical training, creative expression, and guidance on being intentional with how we are each practicing. Her movement style was described by The New York Times as “grounded, silken.” In addition to contemporary dance, she is currently heavily influenced by house dance, contact improvisation, and mindfulness practices. She is currently on faculty at Shawl-Anderson Dance Center and teaches around the Bay Area, including ODC, the Berkeley Alembic, and Finnish Hall. Zan has previously taught extensively at Gibney, Elon University, ADF studios, and many more. She has shown her choreography in NY, NC, CA, AZ, MA, and MO, and performed in works by Ishika Seth, Mo Miner, and others. Beyond the studio, Suzanne is a facilitator and has worked as a DEI consultant. She also enjoys exploring writing, visual art, nature, music, and belonging. Education: MFA in Dance, NYU Tisch School of the Arts; BA in Geology, UC Berkeley Learn more about Suzanne, upcoming classes/workshops (contemporary, embodiment, improvisation, contact improvisation and private lessons): IG @suzannebeahrs suzannebeahrs.com
