"I wouldn't be the artist-author I am today without A State of Change . I consider Cunningham's work to be an original inspiration for all that I do." --Obi Kaufmann Originally published in 2010, A State of Change: California’s Forgotten Landscapes by Laura Cunningham is widely considered a classic text of California natural history. Returning to print in a fully restyled package in fall 2026, this updated edition includes expanded content, Cunningham’s original oil paintings and field sketches, and a contemporary design that offers readers a firsthand look at pre-colonial California and the immense biodiversity that once reigned. Melding science, Traditional Ecological Knowledge, stunning landscapes and species portraiture, artist-naturalist Cunningham takes a multi-field perspective to reenvision the West as it once was, before centuries of settlement reshaped the land and its native wildlife. Compiled over decades, A State of Change (on sale October 13, 2026) draws from fieldwork spanning the state and beyond, Indigenous oral histories and interviews with tribal elders, scientific research in biology and paleontology, and years of artistic study. This deep time exploration of Old California throws into stark relief the engineered landscapes we know today and the diminution of biodiversity already millennia in the making. “This book is my life’s work trying to understand California in the past so that we can protect and help restore the natural and cultural landscapes of this precious state into the future,” says Cunningham, whose acclaimed original publication garnered a California Book Award, a Northern California Book Award, was declared a Best Book of the Year by East Bay Express, and a finalist for Foreword’s Book of the Year. Cunningham’s original publication predicted the explosive development of megafires in California and reacquainted readers with species long since absent from the landscape—from the extinct flightless marine diving goose to the Golden State’s banner grizzly, last seen a century ago. The 2026 edition of A State of Change reflects watershed ecological developments since the book’s original publication. These include the comebacks of California wolves and condors, the resurgence of salmon populations under tribal stewardship, and the gradual reimplementation of Indigenous fire management. Cunningham also challenges popular ideas about regenerative agriculture and livestock grazing, pointing toward pathways to restore native grasslands that underpin the state’s ecosystems. Learning about the plight of species in the past has kindled Cunningham’s lifelong passion for saving species for the future—and with this galvanizing and visually immersive text she aims to alight a kindred spark in the reader. “This wonderful book is a vivid reminder of how things began, and also as a vision of the rich and beautiful world we can work toward in our shared future,” says author Kim Stanley Robinson, “One of Heyday’s best.” "This wonderful book is a vivid reminder of how things began, and also as a vision of the rich and beautiful world we can work toward in our shared future." -- Kim Stanley Robinson "This brings a lost world straight back to life--and one hopes it will help us work to restore it in the real world." -- Bill McKibben Laura Cunningham is an artist-naturalist and award-winning author of A State of Change: California's Forgotten Landscapes. Cunningham studied paleontology and biology at the University of California, Berkeley. She has worked field biology jobs for the California Department of Fish and Game, the United States Geological Survey, and various universities, gaining experience with such species as Owens Valley pupfish, salmon and steelhead trout, Yosemite toads, Panamint alligator lizards, and tule elk. Simultaneously, she taught herself the arts of sketching and oil painting and pursued studies of California's historical ecology. She currently works in the conservation nonprofit field. Her studio is next to Death Valley National Park along the Amargosa River. We meet and greet, then start with a short introduction to opening awareness meditation. We sit for 20 minutes, take a break, practice some slow standing meditations together, take a break, and then sit for another 20 minutes. We end with questions and discussion. Opening awareness is a seated meditation leading to vividness and spacious clarity. It is Evolving Ground’s foundational meditation and is a contemporary version of the Dzogchen practice of shi-ne (shamatha in Sanskrit). The movements come from the Sky Realm Series (Nam'khor in Tibetan). These are Dzogchen long-de practices unique to Evolving Ground. They look and feel quite similar to Qi Gong, though they operate on a different principle: discovery of the nonduality of clarity and bliss, through the experience of “tsal”—embodied awareness as non-ordinary sensation. Attendees need no prior experience. There will be plenty of space for questions, reflections, and group exploration of the practices. This meetup is free to attend. d5078cbb-dce1-4fa7-af0c-6501dec10170: Our Loving Companions is a groundbreaking immersive theater experience celebrating the beautiful bond at the heart of pet ownership. A bond strong enough to propel us through deeply painful loss, time and again. Over 90 minutes, audiences journey through the laughter, devotion, inexplicable joy, and grief that define our relationships with our animal companions. Most shows will have a facilitated discussion afterwards for those who desire to partake. Audience members are encouraged to bring a small photo of their loving companion, past or present, to add to the production’s art installation at the entryway of the theatre. We look forward to helping honor your cherished bond. “The Bridge” by Jay Cross “What We Know” by Stephanie Weisman “A Dog Dreams” by Jeffrey Fisher Smith ”A Little Bird Told Me” by Marilyn Anderson “Must Love Pitbulls” by Jenny Mead “Tomorrow” by Alan Stewart “Outside the Box” by Emily Turner “A Good Dog” by Laura Neill “Ellie’s Goodbye” by Leslie Corn “Like a Dog”by Anya Martin “For The Love Of Buddy” by Dyanna Morrison “Roll Over, a monologue from the cat’s point of view” by Tommy Our Loving Companions is the result of a shared artistic vision between Grief Dialogues founder Elizabeth Coplan and co-producer and playwright Alan Stewart . Recognizing the need for an animal-centered immersive experience, Coplan envisioned a space that honors the distinct and deeply personal nature of the creatures who share our homes, our routines, and our unconditional love. Stewart, a producer, playwright, Dramatist Guild Foundation Fellow, and former trustee of San Francisco’s Magic Theatre, brings a distinctive artistic voice shaped by his first career as a veterinary internist and a lifelong belief in the human-animal bond as a language of the heart. Together, they create theater that invites audiences not only to witness grief, but to experience it in a way that clarifies, deepens, and transforms. As founder and Artistic Director of The Marsh, Stephanie Weisman brings a deep appreciation for work that blends storytelling with emotional truth, making her collaboration with Our Loving Companions a natural and meaningful fit. She is delighted to welcome Grief Dialogues to both The Marsh San Francisco and Berkeley—spaces long dedicated to bold, intimate, and transformative performance. Through hundreds of productions each year, alongside classes, youth programs, and live music, The Marsh has become a home for stories that matter. Stephanie’s own work in grief-centered theater, including her play 180 Days, To Die. To Live. , reflects that same commitment to exploring life’s most tender moments with honesty and care. And at home, her own loving companions—Marsh mascots Marsha and Junior—are never far from heart, a daily reminder of the deep bonds this experience so beautifully honors. Under the consulting direction of Dani Davis , Our Loving Companions living, immersive theatrical experience invites audiences to move through a curated landscape of short plays, poetry, music, sculpture, shared reflection, and personal stories. Blending warmth, tenderness, reverence, and moments of gentle humor, the production explores death, loss, and remembrance through what follows the final goodbye…the empty leash, the quiet food bowl, the space at the foot of the bed. Each performance is carefully choreographed behind the scenes to create an atmosphere fostering connection, validation, and collective witnessing for those grieving animal companions. In a culture where pet loss is sometimes dismissed as “lesser,” this experience affirms that love is not measured by species, and grief is not ranked by hierarchy. Michael Bud serves as Creative Producer and Director of Design for Our Loving Companions , shaping the audience experience from arrival through reflection. Working across promotion, staging, production design, and visual storytelling, he translates the project’s artistic and emotional vision into a cohesive immersive environment. His role supports both the creative flow of each performance and the deeper intention to witness, honor, and hold space for those mourning the loss of cherished animal companions. 14336258-1d2e-4e65-8fe5-de6b2ecf75c8: In a provocative new work blending manifesto, philosophy, and ecological inquiry, the bestselling California Field Atlas series creator challenges readers to reimagine humanity's relationship with the living world. Obi Kaufmann will be joined in conversation by Victoria Schlesinger, the editor-in-chief of Bay Nature. This fall, award-winning creator of the California Field Atlas series, Obi Kaufmann, publishes his most probing and philosophical book to date: California Inside Out: Mapping an Ecology of Mind(on-sale: October 6, 2026). With this compact, pocket-sized volume, the San Francisco Chronicle and Los Angeles Times bestselling author recenters radical kinship with the more-than-human world, advancing an environmental worldview rooted in the recognition of nature’s agency and humanity’s inseparable relationship to place. Part manifesto, part lyrical meditation, California Inside Out interrogates the stories that estrange people from the living systems that surround them and searches for new language capable of restoring that connection. Kaufmann challenges the assumptions that promote extractive thinking and sets out to tell another story; one aimed at helping Californians leave the state at the close of the 21st century healthier, more resilient, and more ecologically whole than it was at the century’s start. Deriving inspiration from Traditional Ecological Knowledge, the lessons of deep time, and the blueprints of renowned naturalists including Aldo Leopold, Gary Snyder, and Robin Wall Kimmerer, Kaufmann sketches the contours of an emergent conservation ethic for the 22nd century. Rejecting the inherited “man versus nature” model, he proposes creative frameworks for realizing equity and mutuality between humans and the wider living world. Kaufmann’s approach is deeply Socratic, inviting readers to consider provocative questions: What if wildfire were revered rather than reviled? What if humans respected the creative capacity of other species? What if watersheds have volition and rivers were accorded legal rights? At the heart of California Inside Out is a quest to find the new premises—or long-forgotten verities—that may reveal enough intrinsic value in nonhuman entities to inspire people to retrieve their responsibility as stewards of the systems upon which all life depends. For the notion that wilderness exists separate from human development is ahistorical, Kaufmann reminds us. “The structural makeup of habitat spaces is largely the product of a consistent, multimillennia-long project of human stewardship,” he observes, invoking Indigenous traditions and technologies that have shaped the American West for thousands of years. Everything from faunal biogeography to soil fecundity has been shaped by human hands, human history, and increasingly, human policy: “California’s landscape is an ecological artifact of human activity.” With California Inside Out, Kaufmann challenges readers to consider what kind of landscape will emerge from continuing along with a now centuries-long protocol of human activity that is driven primarily by extraction and capital utility—and appeals to the reader to ensure that another story, a better story, prevails. "Obi Kaufmann’s books are like bibles to me. They explain California’s natural beauty better than anything I’ve read before.” —DAVE EGGERS “A full immersion into the astonishingly varied natural worlds. Gorgeous.” —CBS SAN FRANCISCO "Obi leaves no leaf unturned in his quest to capture the wonder and fragility.” —SUNSET "Kaufmann’s gaze easily ranges from the micro to the macro. Kaufmann is a former board member of the California Wilderness Coalition and winner of the 2019 Mark Dubois River Protection Award. Notable recent illustration projects include a 2022 residency with the National Wildlife Federation as the illustrator for the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing and a 2025 writing and painting residency for the National Gallery of Art in Yosemite. In 2026 he will participate in an authors' residency in Stockholm with the Swedish Institute. His most recent book is California Inside Out: Mapping an Ecology of Mind (2026). When he is not backpacking, the painter-poet can be found at home in the East Bay, posting trail paintings @coyotethunder on Instagram. Victoria Schlesinger is editor-in-chief of Bay Nature . Schlesinger has worked as a raft guide in Colorado, a backpacking counselor in the Trinity Alps, and spent the better part of her 20s researching and writing a book about ecology in Central America. Her journalism career began at California Wild magazine and the Point Reyes Light newspaper, and she has since earned two master’s degrees from Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism. Her articles have appeared in Harper’s Magazine , Mother Jones , Audubon and The New York Times , among many other outlets, and she’s been on staff with Discover , PBS Frontline, Plenty , and California Lawyer . She lives in Berkeley with her husband and daughter. 39713dcd-d6b6-45cf-afd3-d04f1ca74423: 💥 What could possibly outshine an entire galaxy? Some of the most energetic and fascinating objects in the universe are exploding stars known as supernovae. These huge outbursts come from the violent deaths of stars and can briefly become brighter than the entire galaxy that contains them. The atoms needed to build life are forged inside stars and then scattered across space during these explosions. In this talk, Dr. Jeffrey Silverman, who earned his PhD in Astrophysics at UC Berkeley studying supernovae with Professor Alex Filippenko, explains why these events matter so much to science. Observations of distant supernovae provided the first evidence that the expansion of the universe is actually speeding up rather than slowing down, a completely unexpected discovery tied to one of the biggest unsolved mysteries in modern physics: dark energy. Silverman, now a data scientist and longtime science communicator, brings both his astrophysics background and a talent for public outreach to this exploration of dying stars and the mysteries they leave behind. ✨ 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? In 2023, Escobar sold out venues across the nation with his “Victory Lap” tour — an inspiring experience intended to empower audiences to celebrate their lives and all they’ve overcome. Escobar has a lot to celebrate on his musical journey, with his song “Taboo” earning the #1 song in the country and topping the Billboard charts, as well as the release of his highly anticipated album, Gemini. Escobar is letting it be known that his reign as the King of Strings will not cease. He’s on a mission to prove there’s astonishing power in instrumental music, and he intends to motivate listeners and make an impact on mainstream music like never before. With the release of his studio album, “Gemini”, Escobar is showing no signs of slowing down.

6b260a89-7a4c-47f4-a08c-7aac474082ac: From Snake Oil to Social Media: Deciphering Medical Truths in the Wellness Age Our desire for health, longevity, and bodily control makes us susceptible to the promise of quick cures. Today’s wellness landscape prioritizes algorithmic advice, viral detoxes, and AI diagnoses. Relying on unverified remedies is far from new. To understand how we navigate medical "truth,” we can look across history, psychology, and modern healthcare systems to see how information spreads, why it takes root, and who stands to profit. Join Dominican University faculty members Vivian Delchamps Wolf, Sophie Whynacht, and Michael Skolnik for a panel exploring the boundaries of medicine, wellness, and trust. Drawing connections from 19th-century medicines to modern influencer culture and politicized care, the panelists will examine why mythical cures persist, how digital culture shapes our relationship with our bodies, and how patients can build critical information literacy in an age of digital noise. The 90-minute session will feature short presentations from each panelist followed by an open audience Q&A. This conversation brings together interdisciplinary faculty from Dominican University: Vivian Delchamps Wolf (PhD, UCLA English, 2022) is an Assistant Professor of English at Dominican University of California (DUC). Her research and teaching focus upon 19th-century American literature and feminist disability studies. Peer-reviewed articles have been published or are forthcoming in the J19: The Journal of 19th-Century Americanists, Disability Studies Quarterly, the Emily Dickinson Journal, and Literature and Medicine. Her monograph, Resisting Diagnosis: Women’s Disability Literature of the 19th-Century U.S., argues that women writers use literature to challenge patriarchal medicine and racialized pathologization and to imagine expansive forms of care. Wolf serves or has recently served professional organizations including the Modern Language Association, C19: The Society of Nineteenth-Century Americanists, and the Health Humanities Consortium through conference organizing, committee work, and disability advocacy. Sophie Whynacht, Ph.D. is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Dominican University of California, where she leads the Body Image and Stigma (BIAS) Research Lab. She is also a Licensed Psychologist and the founder of Embodied Psychotherapy and Counseling, a private practice specializing in the clinical treatment of eating disorders, body image concerns, and related mental health challenges. Her academic work centers on the psychological and sociocultural factors that drive body image issues, weight stigma, and disordered eating. Dr. Whynacht’s writing on body image is featured on Psychology Today. Michael Skolnik , Academic Director of the Healthcare Executive MBA program, who brings deep expertise in healthcare leadership, institutional strategy, and the systemic challenges patients face when navigating medicine, technology, and misinformation. Vivian Delchamps Wolf, Sophie Whynacht, Ph.D., Michael Skolnik - photos courtesy of the organizers

Palo Alto for a reading and signing of his new book, Survivor Legends: The Players Who Changed the Game (Unofficial & Unauthorized)! Shaan will be joined by Survivor winner Yul Kwon! About the book: A deep dive into the players who shaped Survivor—and how their stories helped define reality TV. [Book not endorsed by or affiliated with any creator or producer of the show] For more than 25 years, Survivor has reigned supreme as one of the most influential shows on American television. Each season, castaways from across the country arrive on a secluded island with the same ultimate goal: to outwit, outplay, and outlast for the $1 million prize. The game is physically grueling and psychologically unforgiving. While the structure of the game remains familiar, what has made Survivor endure—and evolve—is the players at the center of the it. Survivor Legends tells the stories of the players who left an indelible mark on the series, through narrative profiles that revisit the show’s most influential figures. From early rule-breakers and strategic innovators like Richard Hatch and Cirie Fields, to unlikely heroes and enduring icons, like Parvati Shallow and Mike White, these players didn’t just change how the game was played—they shaped how audiences understood competition, character, and authenticity. Through their stories—who was celebrated, who was vilified, and how those judgments shifted—this book offers fresh insight into beloved contestants while revealing how American ideas about identity, morality, and power have changed across a quarter century of reality television. His work has been featured in the New York Times, Slate, Salon, Washington Monthly, Condé Nast Traveler, Insider, Philadelphia Inquirer , and more. 44e76c13-01b0-471b-b711-3db03af96abf: 💥 What could possibly outshine an entire galaxy? Some of the most energetic and fascinating objects in the universe are exploding stars known as supernovae. These huge outbursts come from the violent deaths of stars and can briefly become brighter than the entire galaxy that contains them. The atoms needed to build life are forged inside stars and then scattered across space during these explosions. In this talk, Dr. Jeffrey Silverman, who earned his PhD in Astrophysics at UC Berkeley studying supernovae with Professor Alex Filippenko, explains why these events matter so much to science. Observations of distant supernovae provided the first evidence that the expansion of the universe is actually speeding up rather than slowing down, a completely unexpected discovery tied to one of the biggest unsolved mysteries in modern physics: dark energy. Silverman, now a data scientist and longtime science communicator, brings both his astrophysics background and a talent for public outreach to this exploration of dying stars and the mysteries they leave behind. ✨ 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? Free to Attend, Please RSVP Or Watch on YouTube Live/Link Available Soon About The Names of the New World The highly anticipated second novel from the award-winning author Kawai Strong Washburn: an extraordinary saga of resilience and ambition in the face of a chaotic world. A ferocious superstorm strikes Minneapolis, obliterating swaths of the city in minutes. In its wake, three people forge an unlikely bond that will shape their lives for the next twenty-five years: Naomi, a lawyer and an amateur MMA fighter, is a Pacific Islander transplanted to the Midwest for her less-than-satisfying career; Amaré, an investment banker, has grand designs for all the money he’s about to make; and Raheem, a diesel mechanic, is nearly paralyzed by the storm and struggles to save his business. When Naomi recognizes that energy companies are responsible for the climate-induced superstorm—and the many more to come, potentially dooming her island homeland—she initiates a bitter legal battle, one that culminates in her appointment to a powerful political office in DC with the potential to prevent future tragedies. Yet her rise risks a burgeoning romance with Amaré, whose own ambitions test Naomi’s ethical limits, while Raheem’s fate as a small business owner depends on the couple’s growing power. Following his much-loved debut, Kawai Strong Washburn turns his gift of mythic sight to the oceans and landscapes we so often overlook in the name of progress. Ranging from the American Midwest to the nation’s halls of power to islands across the Pacific, The Names of the New World is a startling, energetic, and optimistic vision of how we’ll live in this era of overwhelming change. About Kawai Strong Washburn Kawai Strong Washburn was born and raised on the Hāmākua coast of the Big Island of Hawai‘i. Today, he lives with his wife and daughters in Minneapolis. Sharks in the Time of Saviors, his first novel, was a New York Times Notable Book and winner of the PEN/Hemingway Award.
580f602f-3ee7-442a-b7e5-8ad413c194bb: FREE Part of Words Around the World Sponsored by Center for the Art of Translation Co-presented with City Lights and New York Review of Books First published in 1922, and rich in startling neologisms and other forms of verbal play, Trilce is a blazingly vivid revelation of what poetry can be, at once a love poem, a poem of erotic urgency and frustration, a poem of family life, of political fury, a lament for the dead, a work of intense privacy and an address to the world. In this new edition of Trilce from NYRB—the recipient of the prestigious Premio Valle Inclán for the best translation from Spanish into English—the translators Helen Dimos and William Rowe accompany each poem with a gloss. Their incisive commentary on these legendarily challenging poems opens them up to new understanding while inviting readers to find their own pathways to and through them.
7b9cf6e4-3eeb-4997-bae9-e52cd27030eb: 🌍 Why does something as urgent as climate change leave so many of us paralyzed instead of motivated? Climate change is not just a problem of engineering and policy. At its core, it is a product of human thought, behavior, and motivation, which means psychology has something important to say about it. Join Gregory Feist, Professor of Psychology at San José State University, for a look at why so many people either deny the crisis outright or freeze up when confronted with its scale. Drawing on decades of research into creativity, motivation, and the psychology of science, Feist will unpack the mental habits and biases that make climate change uniquely hard for our brains to process. He will also explore what basic psychological principles suggest about breaking through denial and inaction, and how that understanding might translate into real solutions. This talk offers a grounded, evidence-based way to think about one of humanity's biggest challenges, from the inside out. 🌱 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? 7ba88828-dde1-461e-bbd1-8b66e9be96cd: What Earthlings should expect. · The Moon inspires myth, song, poems, and journeys. Mysterious and elegant, it lights the night, generates tides, and affects Earth’s climate. Since human beginnings, the Moon has been our common heritage owned by no one, shared by all peoples; a revered object, not a destination. And yet, in the present, global forces race and compete to claim lunar resources. What plans are underway? Do the peoples of our planet have a say? Can poetry, or any art, make a difference? What will it be like to look up at an inhabited Moon? When she found out that a poem would be sent to the Moon in a time capsule, former Santa Clara County Poet Laureate Sally Ashton realized her resistance to the forces of lunar exploitation is in very real conflict with her excitement at being part of a lunar landing. Her book, Going to the Moon , explores this paradox and the fraught relationship of humans with conquest and the non-human world. Join her conversation with Dr. Persis Karim, faculty emerita at San Francisco State University, as they ponder the Moon, consider the progress of the lunar goldrush, and explore our role in the revived race to space at this transformational moment in human history—the colonization of the Moon. Sally Ashton is a poet, writer, teacher, and editor-in-chief of DMQ Review , an online journal featuring poetry and art. Publishing in three genres, she is the author of five books of poems including Listening to Mars (Cornerstone Press, 2024). San José State University faculty emerita, she continues to teach workshops locally and online. Her poem “4.6 Billion Years” is archived on the Moon with the Lunar Codex. The author of the global sensation Lessons in Chemistry returns with an irresistible, delightful, and tender literary novel set in the publishing world of 1980s New York City about a young man whose life turns upside down when he is hired by the most prestigious, secretive, and dysfunctional poetry journal in the world: the renowned Peck & Peck . Presented in partnership with Calvary Presbyterian San Francisco A MOST ANTICIPATED BOOK FOR COUNTRY LIVING AND BOOKPAGE Find originality. Reward creativity. Burn the rest. It’s 1982, New York City. Crime is on the rise, muggings are in the streets, and Batter Gray, recent college graduate with a skill that no one wants—an “ear” for poetry—is worried about his future. While all of his friends have real jobs, he’s folding T-shirts at the Gap. As for love? No. Not unless you count Sallie Mae, the student loan tyrant. He hears from Sallie all the time. But when Batter gets a dream job at Peck & Peck , the most prestigious poetry quarterly in the world, his life moves into the literary fast lane. Soon Batter is knee-deep in the secret war between the two Editors in Chief, the famous Peck brothers—twins and enemies—as well as being privy to the private affairs of their thirty-nine editors, whose professed mission is the same: Find originality. Reward creativity. Burn the rest. And by burn, they mean incinerate. Because at Peck & Peck , “good” isn’t good enough, “interesting” doesn’t cut it, plagiarists aren’t tolerated, and parolees run the mailroom. Still want to submit your poem? Go with God. Welcome to another dazzling and unforgettable novel from Bonnie Garmus. If you loved Lessons in Chemistry , you will love Peck & Peck. “Tender-hearted… [Garmus] packs the novel with the antic humor and colorful characterizations that drew readers to her debut. There’s much to cherish in this charming tale.” — Publishers Weekly “[People are] hungry for another Bonnie Garmus hit. Thankfully Peck & Peck is here to feed those gaping mouths... It is EXACTLY what I needed to read right now. Charming, uplifting, soulful, and original, this is the perfect successor to Lessons in Chemistry . If you loved Elizabeth Zott, you will adore Batter Gray. Book clubs will adore this novel. I loved it." —Kristin Hannah, #1 New York Times bestselling author of The Nightingale and The Women Bonnie Garmus is a coffee-dependent American novelist. Her debut novel, Lessons in Chemistry , was a Good Morning America Book Club Pick, a Goodreads Choice Best Book of the Year, spent nearly two years on the New York Times bestseller list and was named by Times readers as one of the top 100 books of the 21st century. Translated into over forty languages, Lessons in Chemistry was honored with sixteen international literary awards and made into an Apple TV limited series. Peck & Peck is her second novel. KATE SCHATZ is a feminist author, educator, and public speaker. She's the New York Times- bestselling author of the "Rad Women" book series; the novel Where the Girls Were; the 33 ⅓ book Rid of Me: A Story ; and Do the Work: An Anti-Racist Activity Book , co-written with W. Kamau Bell. She lives in the Bay Area with her wife, three children, and pets. In all she does, Kate is committed to sharing radical histories that shine light on the marginalized people who've truly made America (and the world) great: the people of color, the immigrants, the queers, the punks, the weirdos, the artists, the workers, and the women. 2253dbe6-0e6a-4dd9-9468-de8740632969: In this deeply experiential yoga practice, we will explore the dynamic interplay between stability and mobility, strength and relaxation, movement and stillness. Through mindful movement, standing and seated practices, breath, and attention to the subtle ways we organize ourselves in space, we'll investigate what allows us to feel both grounded and free. This event happens each week at the Alembic. Rather than striving for perfect alignment or mastering difficult poses, we'll approach the practice as an exploration. We'll slow down enough to notice, experiment with different possibilities, and discover how the balance between effort and ease can change our experience of movement — and of ourselves.. Teacher Bio: Vickie Russell Bell has been teaching yoga for more than 30 years, bringing together the precision of alignment-based yoga with a deep curiosity about how we inhabit our bodies, regulate our nervous systems, and move through the world. She is an E-RYT 500 and Certified Yoga Therapist (C-IAYT), and has studied with some of the most respected teachers in the Iyengar-influenced yoga tradition. Her teaching is grounded in the belief that yoga is less about mastering poses than developing a more intimate relationship with ourselves. Her classes invite students to slow down, pay attention, and explore the constantly shifting relationships between stability and mobility, strength and softness, effort and ease. She teaches students of all ages and abilities, with a particular interest in yoga as a practice for living fully and well over time.
5e4a11eb-604f-4367-9286-58a8eef6ca01: Every Tuesday morning, the Alembic opens for a half-day of silent meditation practice. This is an unguided silent retreat consisting of three 40-minute meditation periods. There will be no teacher-led instruction during the meditation periods. Participants are invited to bring and engage in their own silent meditation practice. Whether you practice mindfulness, Zen, Vipassana, contemplation, prayer, or another silent form of meditation, all are welcome. The retreat begins promptly at 9:30 AM and concludes at 11:50 AM. Please arrive between 9:15 AM and 9:25 AM to remove your shoes, settle in, and find a seat before the first bell. The morning is divided into three periods of silent meditation: 9:30 AM – 10:10 AM 10:20 AM – 11:00 AM 11:10 AM – 11:50 AM A bell will signal the beginning and end of each meditation period. The meditation hall (Sol) is reserved for silent practice during sitting periods. Between sits, participants may quietly stretch, visit the restroom, or spend time in the tearoom. Conversation is permitted during breaks; however, we encourage participants to keep voices low, as some attendees choose to observe silence throughout the entire morning. You are welcome to leave the meditation hall at any time if needed. If you leave during a meditation period, please wait until the next break before re-entering. We ask that all entrances and exits be as quiet and unobtrusive as possible. This is a “Bring Your Own Silent Meditation” retreat. We provide the structure and the space; you provide your own silent practice. Participants may choose to sit in Sol or engage in quiet movement practice in the tearoom during meditation periods. To minimize disruption, please enter Sol only during the transition periods between sits. If you arrive after a meditation period has begun, you are welcome to practice elsewhere in the Alembic until the next bell. The suggested donation is $10. No one will be turned away for lack of funds. We do ask that all attendees register through the Momence app or via the registration link on the Alembic website. Please note that the retreat ends at 11:50 AM, and we ask all participants to depart by 12:00 PM so that our volunteer teacher and staff may close the space in a timely manner. Thank you for helping us maintain a quiet and supportive environment for practice.

eafa3d97-927a-448b-bd65-4580032a8f65: We are honored to welcome Erin French to Calvary Presbyterian for an afternoon celebrating the release of The Lost Kitchen Volume 3: Seize the Supper. The stunning third volume in The Lost Kitchen cookbook series from Erin French, award-winning restaurant founder and New York Times -bestselling author of Finding Freedom, The Lost Kitchen, and Big Heart Little Stove Erin will be joined in conversation by Tanya Holland, the author of Tanya Holland's California Soul: Recipes from a Culinary Journey West [A Cookbook]. Presented in partnership with Calvary Presbyterian San Francisco Erin French brings you perfectly crafted meals for dining outside the box and living in the moment in her latest cookbook, Seize the Supper . From her beloved home and restaurant, the Lost Kitchen in Freedom, Maine, come hearty main dishes balanced with crisp, bright salads and sweet and spiced desserts. Her well-rounded meals are made with true comfort and seasonal nourishment that are perfect for carrying you from shorter days and late-afternoon feasts to snowy winter nights sitting by the fire to picnics that welcome the blooming of spring. In simple yet rewarding steps, French shares delicious recipes that will foster connection and inspiration around the table. From flavorful salads and sides such as Soft Polenta with Honey & Ricotta, Roasted Asparagus with Tarragon Vinaigrette, and Pear, Walnut & Blue Cheese Waldorf to rich mains including Provençal Roasted Chicken, Fried Halibut, and Buttermilk Leg of Lamb with Fennel & Orange to irresistible desserts like Baked Vanilla Spice Puddings with Cherry Compote and Rosemary Maple Ice Cream, French’s recipes are filled with warmth, heart, and meaningful tips for embracing the joy of now. Erin French , a born-and-raised Mainer, is the owner and chef of the Lost Kitchen, a fifty-seat restaurant in Freedom, Maine, listed among Time ’s World’s Greatest Places to visit and Bloomberg ’s " 12 Restaurants Worth Traveling Across the World to Experience.” With two New York Times bestsellers to her name, Finding Freedom and Big Heart Little Stove , Erin is featured in three seasons of the Magnolia Network series The Lost Kitchen and Getting Lost with Erin French, where she travels the country searching for new experiences and culinary inspiration, streaming on HBO Max. Erin knows the importance of simple pleasures found in gathering for thoughtfully prepared meals. Her love of Maine and sharing its delicious heritage with dinner guests has garnered several James Beard nominations and the attention of The New York Times , Martha Stewart Living, The Wall Street Journal, The Boston Globe, and Food & Wine, as well as NPR’s All Things Considered, CBS News Sunday Morning, and Today. After more than a decade in business, the Lost Kitchen has become so much more than a restaurant, now boasting a farmer’s market, overnight cabins, a retail shop, and a café called the Little Lost Kitchen. Tanya Holland is an award-winning chef, restaurateur, cookbook author, educator, media personality, wine professional, and U.S. State Department Culinary Diplomat. A French-trained chef with more than four decades of experience, she is best known as the founder and executive chef of Oakland’s Brown Sugar Kitchen, where she earned national recognition for modern African American cuisine and thoughtful, inclusive hospitality. Holland is the author of Brown Sugar Kitchen and Tanya Holland’s California Soul and has appeared on Food Network’s Melting Pot, Bravo’s Top Chef, and other programs. Her work has been featured in The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, Bon Appétit, Gourmet, House Beautiful, and O, The Oprah Magazine. She serves on the James Beard Foundation Board of Trustees and, in 2026, joined the University of Virginia as a Senior Lecturer. Across food, wine, teaching, media, and diplomacy, Holland creates memorable experiences that bring people together around the table. 7d6e2486-480b-4c7e-a1ac-1947fd73c06d: A taut, emotionally gripping, and surprisingly funny novel about a father and daughter stranded in an airport at the end of the world, Passengers is a story of loving across gaps—between parent and child, between things said and unsaid—and what happens when the outside world finally mirrors the chaos within. ​This is Maksik’s most timely and accomplished novel yet! Ivan is a solitary man in his seventies, set in his ways and haunted by the failures of his past. His smart and cynical daughter, Nina, is in the twilight of her twenties and has long kept a distance from her sentimental father. But when Ivan proposes a trip to Europe in hopes that it will bring them closer together, Nina reluctantly agrees. They meet at LAX, where their departure is delayed. And delayed again. And again. As the hours drag on, their sharp, caustic and wide-ranging conversation reveals a lifetime of misunderstandings, unhealed wounds, and stubborn love. Soon more flights are canceled, security tightens, airport staff grow evasive, and it becomes clear to Ivan and Nina that something is wrong. They begin to suspect that they’re being held prisoner—sequestered from the world without explanation. At last, the surreal starts to overtake the mundane, and their need to escape—and to protect each other—turns increasingly urgent. What begins as a piercing portrait of a father and daughter becomes a novel of eerie suspense, as Nina and Ivan navigate not only their fractured bond but also a world teetering on the brink of collapse. A story of loving across gaps—between parent and child, between things said and unsaid—and about what happens when the outside world finally mirrors the chaos within, Passengers is Maksik’s most timely and accomplished novel yet. “A beautiful, unsettling novel about the depths of love, the burden of nostalgia and the maddening impossibility of translating feeling into language.”—Imbolo Mbue, author of Behold the Dreamers “A novel of surpassing beauty and among the most moving portraits of parenthood I’ve ever read. It also happens to be exceptionally funny, propulsive and wise—an example of the alchemy that occurs when a writer finds the work he was born to pursue. Passengers is Alexander Maksik’s masterpiece.”—Anthony Marra, author of Mercury Pictures Presents "Maksik's best to date. Passengers is really about how we're all trying to get somewhere different, somewhere better--to a place where we can be closer to those we love, during this one precious life we have. I could not put it down."—Adam Ross “This is the stuff we live for—a spinning dream of a book, pure heart-in-your-throat magic. I can’t say this enough: read it, today, now.”—Paul Yoon, author of The Hive and the Honey , winner of The Story Prize “ Passengers is a tour de force that reveals just how deeply two ordinary people can love one another…This superb novel takes on the very hardest stuff of life and never looks away.”—Ben Fountain, author of Billy Lynn’s Long Halftime Walk “Maksik’s latest, Passengers, is propulsive and fierce and uncompromising in its humanity. And funny too, in often unexpected ways. Also, my kind of book in that it doesn’t waste a single word. It's kept me intensely good company these past few weeks. Seems to me: A necessary book for these batshit times.”—Peter Orner Alexander Maksik is the author of You Deserve Nothing , a New York Times and IndieBound bestseller; A Marker to Measure Drift , which was a New York Times Notable Book, as well as a finalist for the William Saroyan Prize and Le Prix du Meilleur Livre Étranger, and the basis of the 2023 motion picture Drift ; Shelter in Place , named one of the best books of the year by the Guardian and the San Francisco Chronicle; and The Long Corner , a New York Times Book Review Editor’s Choice, and named one of the best books of the year by The Australian . In the tiny town of Pine Hollow, barista and fledging sorceress Talula Smith runs The Blue Moon Café & 24-Hour Occult Emporium, aka the worst coffee shop in town. The café's horrible reputation hides its true purpose: providing new identities and safe passage to at-risk magical beings while keeping humans far, far away. That is, except for town local Dahlia. Dahlia's devastating dimples, addiction to Talula's cocoa recipe, and keen observation skills keeps the smitten barista scrambling to ensure that her magical abilities (or, lack thereof) stay a secret. But when big game hunters start preying on magical beings, her powerful sorceress mother is called away to track them down, leaving Talula and her barely-there magic in charge of The Blue Moon. With the impending Samhain festival to organize, magical refugees to help, half of the town turning against her, and her ever-growing feelings for Dahlia, Talula's magical destiny feels further away than ever. But as the hunters set their sights closer to home, it'll be up to Talula to master her craft, trust her heart, and bring her magical and human communities together . . . before she loses everything she loves. "You're in for a treat! The Blue Moon Café & 24-Hour Occult Emporium is deliciously delightful and absolutely adorable! I loved it!" -Sarah Beth Durst, New York Times bestselling author of The Spellshop Lexie Sharabianlou earned her Master’s in creative writing from the University of Edinburgh. Instead, a disastrous setup and an awkward run-in with her ex-best friend Robbie leave her wishing for a holiday miracle. Glamorous? Sure. Perfect? Not so much. Between caroling and cookie baking, Marygrace is checking exes off her list—but somehow, Robbie keeps showing up too. Maybe the love she’s been searching for has been there all along ... With a sprinkling of sugar and just the right amount of spice, this romance about family, friendship, finding your voice, and the promise of “what-if” is a holiday treat you won’t want to miss. “An enjoyable time-loop holiday rom-com about choosing one’s own path and finding one’s voice.” — Library Journal C.C. 20074eee-84d2-4e76-aeea-26881d8e8c4b: 🌊 What if the boundaries we impose on nature prevent us from seeing how it actually works? Scientists often divide the natural world into neat categories: ocean and seafloor, land and water, surface and subsurface. But nature rarely follows those boundaries, and the categories we create can shape what we notice, what we miss, and what we choose to protect. Geological oceanographer Ivano Aiello explores this idea through three surprising case studies. At the bottom of the Mediterranean, an extraordinary ecosystem blurs the line between ocean and seafloor. In Monterey Canyon, repeated maps reveal a landscape that is constantly being reshaped. And after the Moss Landing battery fire, the way scientists defined something as simple as the “surface” determined whether contamination was detected or missed. Together, these stories reveal how the boundaries we create can change what we see, what we understand, and how we respond to our messy, interconnected natural world. 🌍 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? d4ac5abd-0a8f-4197-bcae-e81235a58320: 💘 What if everything evolutionary psychology told you about dating was wrong? For decades, a buzzy branch of science has spread a deeply flawed story about romantic relationships, cloaking itself in the language of incontrovertible Darwinian fact. Evolutionary psychology claims our minds were shaped by primal drives that pit the genders against each other, from the myth that men are wired to be promiscuous to the notion that wealth, status, and beauty are the ultimate aphrodisiacs. In this talk, UC Davis psychology professor Paul Eastwick, author of Bonded by Evolution and co-host of the Love Factually podcast, draws on original experiments from his own lab to reveal that these stories bear little resemblance to how attraction really works. Success in relationships does not hinge on finding the universally good partner, he argues, but on compatibility. Popularity may shape first impressions, but its influence fades fast. And once we look at what men and women actually want, the supposed gender differences tend to evaporate. Eastwick reveals attraction as a process of finding, and often creating, a compatible connection. 💫 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-8:00 --> arrival & chats 8:00-8:40 --> lecture 8:40-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? dea495c1-21de-4aa2-bc62-b842ae1c253b: 🤖 How did a set of math rules from the 1940s end up defining what it means to be rational? In the 1940s, mathematicians and engineers set out to build machines that could make critical decisions under uncertainty. Within a decade, they had invented tools that not only launched modern computer science but quietly rewrote what it means for a human being to make a "rational" choice. Benjamin Recht, a professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences at UC Berkeley, will draw on his new book The Irrational Decision to trace how these academic rules for machines came to define rationality in economics, public policy, and everyday culture. Ben will walk through where automated decision systems have thrived, from accelerating computers to regulating pharmaceuticals to powering e commerce, and where they break down. The pattern he has found is consistent: these systems excel in well defined spaces with clear rules and measurable goals, and turn brittle or absurd outside them. The talk will close with a genuinely open question. How do we keep using these powerful tools without surrendering human judgment and agency in the process? 🧮 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? f322fb2d-759a-47db-beab-68c095ecb36c: Join us to celebrate Sonny Buttar's stunning debut novel, The Daughters of Rosebud . This multigenerational family saga will leave you at once heartbroken and hopeful. Sonny will be joined in conversation by Vanessa Hua , bestselling author of Coyoteland. This event is FREE to attend. Seating is first-come, first-served. (RSVPs are optional, but encouraged for our planning purposes.) About the Book: In a heart-wrenching debut, author Sonny Buttar delivers a multigenerational family saga at once haunting and hopeful. Teacher Salma Chaudhry lives a quiet life, avoiding all attachments. But after a call from her estranged father, the protective shell she lives within starts to crack and the trauma she's buried for eighteen years emerges. Salma and her older sister Asma were inseparable growing up in small-town Rosebud. While Asma was bold and fearless, Salma tried to keep the peace in their fractured family. But amid their mother's decline and their parents' rigid expectations, Asma makes a choice that tears the family apart. The fallout changes everything--and forces Salma to choose between her sister and her parents. Salma has spent years trying to forget. But as she recollects her past and considers reconciliation with her father, a young student opens a surprising connection to Asma's past. In finally facing her history, Salma finds the bravery to love and hope again. The Daughters of Rosebud is a powerful exploration of sisterhood, family loyalty, and the courage it takes to heal. About the Author: Sonny Buttar was born in Pakistan and raised in England and the American Midwest. Her first novel, The Daughters of Rosebud, will be released in October 2026. About the Conversation Partner: Vanessa Hua is the nationally bestselling author of Coyoteland, A River of Stars and Forbidden City , and the story collection Deceit and Other Possibilities , a New York Times Editors’ Pick. A National Endowment for the Arts Literature Fellow, she has also received a Rona Jaffe Foundation Writers’ Award, the Asian/Pacific American Award for Literature, a California Arts Council Fellowship, and a Steinbeck Fellowship in Creative Writing, as well as honors from the de Groot Foundation, the Society of Professional Journalists, and the Asian American Journalists Association. She was a finalist for the California Book Award, the Northern California Book Award, and the New American Voices Award. Previously, she was an award-winning columnist for the San Francisco Chronicle . She teaches at the Warren Wilson MFA Program, Sewanee Writers Conference, and elsewhere. This fall, she is an Ann-Getty Endowed Visiting Artist-Scholar at the University of San Francisco. Her debut narrative nonfiction, Uprooted, is forthcoming.

Nara Aziza Smith is a globally recognized lifestyle creator, entrepreneur, and model. 39fbf402-efca-48c0-ba29-ceb6f61be6d1: Jad Youssef is chef patron of the award-winning Lebnani in Reigate, Surrey which Jay Rayner highly praised in The Observer: ‘one taste of its gloriously zingy Lebanese flavours and you know you’re in the right place.’ Jad was born in Beirut during the Lebanese Civil War, the youngest of six siblings. He learnt to cook in his mother Khadija’s kitchen and in his father’s pastry shop before training at the Ecole Hoteliere in Beirut. After early work in local hotels and restaurants, he moved to Oslo in 2000 as Head Chef at Jeppe Restaurant, later relocating to London to lead the kitchen at Fakhreldine in Piccadilly and serve as Executive Chef at the Levant Group. In 2009, Youssef founded Yalla Yalla in Soho, one of London’s first Lebanese street food restaurants, expanding to Fitzrovia and Shoreditch in the following years. The restaurant received wide critical attention and achieved a cult following. His signature dish, Sawda Djej (chicken livers with pomegranate molasses), developed an equally devoted following and was named one of Time Out London's "100 Best Dishes." After time in Hong Kong, Youssef and his wife Aga returned to the UK to open Lebnani in Reigate, Surrey, in 2020. The restaurant was named Best Restaurant in Surrey by Muddy Stilettos in 2024, awarded an AA Rosette, and was the recipient of the Be Inclusive Hospitality Middle Eastern Food Award in 2025. Jad has also appeared at Meatopia, Taste of London, and Taste of Hong Kong, served as a judge on Celebrity MasterChef UK, appeared on BBC's MasterChef, and worked with Miele among many others. His work has been featured in The Times, The Observer, Financial Times, The Guardian, and numerous other publications. Lebnani - In Lebnani , celebrated chef Jad Youssef invites readers to experience the warmth, generosity and soul of Lebanese cooking through recipes passed down through generations of his family. In his debut book, Jad returns to the dishes and memories that shaped his life in Beirut and beyond, celebrating Lebanese food as it is truly lived and eaten. Featuring 84 authentic recipes from his family’s kitchen in Lebanon and his award-winning restaurant Lebnani in Surrey, the book reveals secret spice blends, time-honoured techniques and beloved family dishes that bring people together around the table. Chapters echo the rhythm of daily life - Lebanese Mornings, Mezza at Home, Tabkha (everyday meals), Mashawi (grills), Sandwiche (street wraps), Helweyet (sweets) and Namlieh (the pantry) - reflecting the meals and moments that shape Lebanese identity. Family stories are woven throughout, tracing how food sustained Lebanese families through conflict, change and celebration. From gathering wild za’atar to mornings spent collecting trays of freshly baked mana’eesh, Jad’s memories root Lebanese cuisine in gratitude, connection and resilience. With evocative imagery and heartfelt storytelling, Lebnani offers a rich portrait of a culture where food, memory and family life are deeply intertwined.

During the evening, we will: Enter a brief guided relaxation Listen to a short, curated music passage Express what surfaces through drawing and writing Share and witness in the group (optional) Leave with a deeper understanding or perspective Rooted in the Bonny Method, this circle draws on Guided Imagery and Music (GIM), developed by Helen Bonny from her work with LSD-assisted therapy at the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center in the 1960s and 70s. Bonny found that music paired with deep relaxation could open the same expanded states she observed in psychedelic sessions, and that the imagery work done afterward carried much of the lasting change. GIM's approach to music and imagery now informs how integration is supported across modern psychedelic-assisted therapy. Please arrive no later than 7pm. Doors lock at 7:10pm. Sophia Wang is a violinist, board-certified music therapist (MT-BC), integration practitioner, and life coach whose work centers on music, imagery, and non-ordinary states of consciousness. With over a decade of clinical experience across oncology, palliative care, and mental health settings, she draws on Guided Imagery and Music, expressive arts, and depth-oriented inquiry to support emotional healing, insight, and meaningful change. Sophia works with people across a wide range of inner terrain: those in cancer care or facing the end of life; people moving through grief, depression, or anxiety; and high-performing professionals and seekers drawn to deep self-inquiry and the integration of transformative experiences. Her approach blends clinical training with creative exploration, emphasizing safety, pacing, and integration.

773bf904-115d-47d3-936c-5ef1219b9d2f: Local author Fleisher presents his gripping historical novel based on the life of little-known naturalist Eugene Marais. Join us at Mrs. Dalloway's Bookstore on Wednesday, October 21 at 7:00 PM when Berkeley author Seth Fleisher comes to the store to launch his new novel The Farther Shore. Seth will be joined by Mindela Ruby for the conversation and will sign copies of his book after the presentation. The Farther Shore is a sweeping novel about fathers and sons, memory and race, and the dangerous fictions that shape us—inspired by the true story of Eugene Marais, one of history's most extraordinary and forgotten minds. Southern Africa, 1890s. Eugene Marais is a brilliant naturalist and iconoclastic journalist whose evolving theories about memory, addiction, and the hive mind are decades ahead of their time. But when tragedy strikes, he abandons his newborn son and disappears into a remote South African forest—leaving behind his child and his conscience, and embarking on research that will haunt both their lives. Thirty years later, his son Charles—now a professor of ancient Buddhist history at Harvard—discovers that his father's work has been weaponized. University faculty are mining Eugene's research to bolster theories of racial hierarchy, and their ambitions are growing darker by the day. Accompanied by a mysterious Jewish graduate student whose fate is becoming entangled with his own, Charles will make an epic journey across continents to heal his fractured past and stop a sinister plot quietly taking root at the world's most prestigious institution. Set across two interlocking timelines—from the British concentration camps of the Boer War to the rising shadow of the Third Reich and WWII— The Farther Shore is a heart-breaking, exhilarating novel about memory, love, and identity, and about the vast distances we’ll travel to find our way home. SETH FLEISHER is an American author whose work has appeared in the Bellevue Literary Review, Pearl, the Journal of Anthropological Research, and elsewhere. Based in Berkeley, California, he has worked with the World Bank Group and other NGOs in South Africa, India, and more than 40 other countries, and co-founded Walk the Walk USA, a U.S.-based democracy initiative to counter the rising tide of authoritarianism. A former Fulbright scholar in Sri Lanka, Seth did Ph.D. work at Harvard in Buddhist social history, a fellowship at Harvard's Center for the Study of World Religions, and a B.A. in literature at Swarthmore, where he and his wife first met in a Chaucer seminar. The Farther Shore is his first novel. MINDELA RUBY is an author, editor and educator. Her novel, Mosh It Up , is about Bay Area garage punk rock. Her prose and poetry appear in T he Dribble Drabble Review, Terrain.org, Santa Monica Review, WomenArts Quarterly, Coachella Review, Rivet: and other outlets plus the anthology Unmasked with a foreword by Gloria Steinem. Her works have been Pushcart and Best Of the Net nominated, including her poetry series Africa Safari Journal (in haiku) (with footnotes). She holds a Ph.D. from UC Berkeley. Her new memoir is currently on submission.

7edd6537-4486-430c-9da6-3c4d052625da: A conversation between fiction writers Donna Miscolta and Marianne Villanueva about where stories come from, what scares them and what makes them laugh when they’re creating characters and situations. Marianne Villanueva, author of four books of dystopian, surreal, and fantasy fiction, will pose questions to Donna Miscolta about her new realist novel Ofelia and Norma . Miscolta, author of four books of fiction, will ask Villanueva about her latest story collection Residents of the Deep . Donna Miscolta’s latest of four books of fiction is Ofelia and Norma . Her stories, essays, and book reviews have appeared in dozens of journals and anthologies. A recording of her work is part of the Library of Congress PALABRA Archive, a showcase for Latin American and Latino writers. She recently moved to Spain and blogs monthly at donnamiscolta.com . Marianne Villanueva is the author of the story collections Ginseng and Other Tales from Manila , Mayor of the Roses , The Lost Language , and Residents of the Deep . A recipient of fellowships from Stanford University and the California Arts Council, she is writing her first novel, set in 16th-century Spain and the Philippines. In Ofelia and Norma , large-bodied twin sisters struggle for a sense of self. When Ofelia sheds pounds from long, solo walks, Norma senses their twinness slipping away. She slips away to an out-of-town college, leaving Ofelia for the first time, and each sister confronts alone life as a large person in an anti-large-person world. Ofelia, having previously lost weight without trying, now makes a deliberate effort to do so, resulting in a disaster that shakes her to her senses. Meanwhile, Norma escapes into her solitude by swimming laps in the college pool where she suffers an experience that sends her into emotional retreat. They move into careers, still estranged until a tender moment leads to the sharing of their secrets and revenge for what one of them has suffered. In Residents of the Deep , Marianne Villanueva explores human resilience in moments of extremity through a series of gripping stories. In “Ice,” two men confront their future in a barren, post-apocalyptic world where survival itself becomes the only meaning: “The point is, there is no point. You just keep going.” In Dumaguete, a young boy is forced to protect his mother, a role that threatens to unravel him. The title story follows a ship captain who discovers a submerged city and is thrust into a moral reckoning that challenges his understanding of responsibility. Clear-eyed and unflinching, these stories reveal the raw tenacity and unyielding spirit of humanity, even in the face of profound vulnerability and hardship.

Crises of capitalism are pushing human civilization toward its breaking points, presenting what sociologist William Armaline calls overlapping threats to human survival: climate change and nuclear war, both potentially made worse by the destabilizing effects of frontier AI. Yet the conversation in Washington and Silicon Valley remains fixated on treating China as our greatest existential rival. In this talk, Armaline, Professor of Sociology and founder of the Human Rights Institute at San José State University, argues that the world cannot survive this great power rivalry. Solving climate change, preventing nuclear war, and regulating dangerous new technologies will require real cooperation and coordination between the United States and China. For the U.S., Armaline says, this means fundamentally rethinking its relationship with China and rejecting the traditional geopolitics of imperial competition. About the Cookbook Acclaimed cookbook author, America's Test Kitchen Editor in Residence, and molecular biologist Nik Sharma brings his deep scientific knowledge, delicious recipes, and stunning photography to home cooks with Fundamentals of Flavor . de77c3a6-65f7-4ed1-bc98-f5224c7fe868: 🌊 Could a supercomputer warn you about a tsunami before the wave even forms? Tsunami early warning systems today rely on models that can take precious minutes to run — minutes that coastal communities don't have. New research is changing that by building a "digital twin" of the earth's crust, one that can simulate the physics of an earthquake and its resulting tsunami in near-real time using some of the most powerful supercomputers on the planet. In this talk, Tzanio Kolev will walk through how his team used Bayesian inversion techniques on the El Capitan supercomputer to model the Cascadia subduction zone — the fault line that threatens the Pacific Northwest with a potentially catastrophic earthquake and tsunami. This work, recognized with the 2025 ACM Gordon Bell Prize, represents a major leap in how we use extreme-scale computing to protect lives. Join us for a look inside the intersection of high-performance computing, applied mathematics, and disaster preparedness — and what it takes to simulate the planet fast enough to matter. 🖥️ 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? dffc38a2-fe08-4e32-a865-8be7d71aebb2: An evening of storytelling with Dead Reckoning · There is an Oakland where the apparition of a woman appears in the mist at Joaquin Miller Park after dark, where the doorbell at the two-story Clarke Mansion at 16th and Castro begins clanging incessantly just after midnight, and where the Camron-Stanford House, one of the last Victorian homes that once lined Lake Merritt, has urged more than one living visitor to "get out." These are just a few of the stories that blur the line between the living and the dead that have lingered in Oakland for generations, passed between those who have witnessed things they still can't explain. Join us for an evening of storytelling with Beth Winegarner and Courtney Minick, hosts of Dead Reckoning : the podcast where death isn't the end of the story. The hosts of the San Francisco-based podcast will share local ghost stories, explore the legends surrounding some of Oakland's most notable residents, and uncover the histories that linger long after death. As the veil grows thin, come prepared to share your own story if you've experienced a haunting in the East Bay. You never know who, or what, might be listening. Courtney Minick is a storyteller with a career spanning technology, law, politics, and creative media based in San Francisco. She is the creator of Here Lies a Story a multi-platform storytelling project that explores history, folklore, and the way the buried past continues to shape our present including the Lost Cemeteries of San Francisco series . Beth Winegarner is a journalist and writer who’s contributed to the New York Times, the New Yorker, The Guardian, and many others. She is the author of several books, most recently San Francisco’s Forgotten Cemeteries: A Buried History and Swim Poems , and she is the co-host of the Dead Reckoning podcast.
e7b53831-dc8c-4e3c-80b8-e99da32bb147: FREE, $10-$15 suggested donation Sponsored by Norway House and Center for the Art of Translation Part of Words Around the World From International Booker Prize– and National Book Award–nominated author Vigdis Hjorth comes her latest novel finally translated into English, Repetition. As winter approaches in Norway and the daylight dwindles, a chance encounter prompts a novelist to reexamine her past. The seismic events following her sixteenth birthday return with haunting vividness, exposing a story both utterly familiar and desperately strange. It was the year she first got drunk, the year she first had sex with a boy. She was watched like a hawk by an anxious mother and a silent, distant father. It was a year of typical teenage fixation and typical teenage frivolity, and of all the usual parental fretting. Until something else took hold, and her family made an unspoken decision and a terrible sacrifice. Only now, decades later, can these events come close to being comprehended. In conversation with Daniela Blei.

Adam will be joined in conversation with Mark Rober, the creator of the STEM subscription box company CrunchLabs. A vibe—a special connection between people that creates a spark—is an engine of happiness and success. Yet building meaningful ties is one of the most pressing problems of our time. As social media forces face-to-face interaction behind digital screens, communication gets outsourced to AI, and the world becomes more polarized than ever, our loneliness crisis shows no signs of slowing. To reveal how we can forge faster, stronger, and longer bonds, Grant offers groundbreaking studies, expert insights, and myth-busting stories. Filled with the eye-opening takeaways that have brought millions of readers to his books, Vibe teaches us that similarity is not necessary for solidarity, chemistry doesn’t always happen quickly, and closeness doesn’t always take time. Along the way, Grant introduces us to a crew of astronauts who learned to trust people they don’t like, a comedy troupe that swears by taking time apart as a key to staying together, a band that grew closer by learning to fight more, and a journalist who designed a gathering that led to seventy-eight marriages. He also opens up about his personal struggles to find his place as a shy introvert and the lessons that propelled his transformation into an enthusiastic convener. Through these examples and more, Grant uncovers the keys to creating deeper relationships and tighter communities. Vibe will change how you approach your interactions. No matter how good you are at connecting, you can always get better—and help others get better too. As an organizational psychologist, Adam Grant is a leading expert on how we can find motivation and meaning, and live more generous and creative lives. He is the author of Think Again, Give and Take, Originals, Option B, and Power Move s and host of the podcast WorkLife. Mark Rober spent nine years as an engineer at NASA before becoming world famous on YouTube for his science and engineering projects. He is creator of the STEM subscription box company CrunchLabs. 6536f3cb-2838-47fc-b328-5d16f2783ec4: Multi-platinum Idol alum known for his big voice · America first fell in love with Clay Aiken's extraordinary voice and undeniable charisma on the second season of American Idol . His journey on the show became a cultural phenomenon, drawing nearly 40 million viewers to the finale—one of the highest-rated live television broadcasts of the 21st century—and launching one of the most successful recording careers to emerge from the series. Aiken's first single, “This Is The Night,” made history as the first track by a brand-new artist to enter the Billboard Hot 100 at No. 1, selling nearly 400,000 copies in its opening week. The follow-up, “Invisible,” became a defining early-2000s pop hit, climbing to No. 37 on the Hot 100 and earning RIAA Gold certification. His debut album, Measure of a Man , then entered the Billboard 200 at No. 1 and went multi-platinum, cementing him as one of pop music's biggest new artists. Among his early highlights was the chart-topping holiday album Merry Christmas with Love , which still holds the record for the largest debut week ever for a holiday album in the SoundScan era. During the first seven years of his recording career, Aiken sold more than six million albums worldwide while becoming a fixture on television and one of the most successful touring artists to emerge from the early 2000s pop era. His rich tenor voice, emotional delivery, and ability to effortlessly move between contemporary pop, adult contemporary, inspirational music, and timeless standards have earned him a loyal, multi-generational audience. Aiken’s career has extended well beyond the recording studio, including a Broadway run in Monty Python’s Spamalot and a reunion with Ruben Studdard in 2018 for Ruben & Clay’s First Annual Christmas Carol Family Fun Pageant Spectacular Reunion Show , which The New York Times hailed as “a Christmas miracle.” The pair reunited once again in 2023 for a tour celebrating the 20th anniversary of their landmark American Idol season before competing together on Fox’s The Masked Singer in 2024 as The Beets. Beyond his music, Aiken has long been an advocate for children with disabilities. Drawing on his pre-fame experience as a special education teacher, he co-founded the National Inclusion Project in 2003, which has since helped thousands of kids with disabilities take part in camps, after-school programs, and community activities in more than 40 states. He also spent a decade as a UNICEF ambassador, traveling to Afghanistan, Somalia, Indonesia, Mexico, Uganda, and Kenya to advocate for children's protection and education. In 2026, Aiken began an exciting new musical chapter with the release of his first new music in eighteen years. His single "Rewind," written by Colton Avery and Grammy Award-winning producer and songwriter Dave Audé and produced by Audé, marked both a return to recording and a fresh creative direction. The release coincided with Aiken's homecoming to the American Idol stage, where he debuted the song during the season finale. As he reintroduces himself to longtime fans and new listeners alike, Aiken is once again focused on what has always defined his career: exceptional songs, unforgettable performances, and one of the most recognizable voices in popular music. "Rewind" is the first offering from a new full-length studio album, due at the end of 2026, his first in nearly two decades.

af63542e-bd6a-4f25-9a10-ea4cd2bca432: Embodiment Practices is an invitation to practice giving ourselves permission to arrive fully to where we are, and gently explore movement and stillness to care for our bodies and ourselves. This event happens each week at the Alembic. As an element of self attunement, we will practice making intuitive choices through a lens of self love, meaning that we are each making choices that are nourishing and responsive to ourselves as individuals in that moment. Part of this practice includes being very intentional and explicit about what kinds of choices we might consider, and being curious about how it feels to try them. There will be many options provided throughout, with guidance around how to navigate choice making, including if this is new to you or you are navigating a limitation or injury. There will be a corner of the room set aside in case you’d like to opt out of the facilitated structure and take a moment for yourself to rest. Opening Circle: We'll ground and check-in with whatever feels present for each of us. We get to welcome ourselves to come as we are. Warm Up: We'll do a guided, full-bodied warm up, tuning the instruments of our bodies and attention, giving ourselves time to shake it out, stretch, wiggle, and move through whatever feels stuck. Movements will be simple enough to follow along, giving us a chance to get out of our heads and drop into our bodies, regulating our nervous system. Drawing on contemporary dance and yoga, there will be flow, rhythm, and music. Movement Explorations: We'll explore movements that deepen our connection with our bodies and our intuition, focusing on concepts and areas of the body that can help us settle and release. Meditation: Finally, we'll settle into meditation and rest. Finding stillness might be sitting/standing/lying down and might include cozy props, having eyes open or closed, and suggestions to make yourself comfortable, including allowing some body movement within that quiet space. Please bring clothes you feel comfortable to move in. It’s recommended to bring long sleeves, long pants and socks with you, in case we are moving on the floor. Bring a journal if you’d like. About Suzanne (Zan): With three decades of contemporary/modern dance experience and 15 years of teaching, Suzanne Beahrs guides students in exploring movement as a pathway to deeper connection—with ourselves, our surroundings, and each other. Her classes blend technical training, creative expression, and guidance on being intentional with how we are each practicing. Her movement style was described by The New York Times as “grounded, silken.” In addition to contemporary dance, she is currently heavily influenced by house dance, contact improvisation, and mindfulness practices. She is currently on faculty at Shawl-Anderson Dance Center and teaches around the Bay Area, including ODC, the Berkeley Alembic, and Finnish Hall. Zan has previously taught extensively at Gibney, Elon University, ADF studios, and many more. She has shown her choreography in NY, NC, CA, AZ, MA, and MO, and performed in works by Ishika Seth, Mo Miner, and others. Beyond the studio, Suzanne is a facilitator and has worked as a DEI consultant. She also enjoys exploring writing, visual art, nature, music, and belonging. Education: MFA in Dance, NYU Tisch School of the Arts; BA in Geology, UC Berkeley Learn more about Suzanne, upcoming classes/workshops (contemporary, embodiment, improvisation, contact improvisation and private lessons): IG @suzannebeahrs suzannebeahrs.com
