cd829900-e541-4f30-8162-2cc6f9fb497b: Join Books Inc. Alameda for our First Saturday Storytime. This month we are thrilled to present author, Martha Freeman, reading and signing copies of her new book, Kitty vs. Christmas. About the book: Kitty is back—but that doesn't mean he's ready for the holidays! The most wonderful time of the year fills this finicky feline with dread. Can Santa help Kitty feel the Christmas spirit? Kitty is a good, nice kitty with a good, nice family who has everything he could ever want. He has his raggedy one-eyed mouse, breakfast at 7:00, supper at 7:00, and a so-cozy life that should never change. But to Kitty’s everlasting surprise and annoyance, things continue to change around him! So when the holiday season arrives, Kitty is not excited. He doesn’t like the itchy sweaters, his family doesn’t appreciate him singing along to Christmas carols, and he’s not even allowed to eat the cookies left right out in the open on Christmas Eve! So Kitty tangles the tinsel, wrecks the wreath, and messes up the mistletoe. Kitty doesn’t feel bad until he sees what a rough night Santa has had. As he and Santa show one another kindness, Kitty realizes that Christmas might not be so bad after all. Martha Freeman was born in Southern California shortly after the Big Bang. As the universe cooled and the Earth formed, Martha grew up and fought injustice, mostly with her pen but sometimes with her feet. Martha has worked as a newspaper reporter, copy editor, substitute teacher, college lecturer, advertising copywriter, and freelance magazine writer. In 1995, she published her first book for children, STINK BOMB MOM (not an autobiography). Subsequently, she has published 30 more books, most recently ZAP! a techno-thriller about a power blackout, and IF YOU'RE GOING TO A MARCH, the perfect how-and-why picturebook for kids on their way to a protest. Besides writing, Martha enjoys running, parallel parking, making pies, hiking and talking on the phone to her far-flung children.

Northern California author Kirk Lombard will be at Mrs. Dalloway's Bookstore chatting with his fans and signing copies of his book The Shadow Stream . He'll be at the store on Saturday, December 5 from 2:00 PM - 3:00 PM so come on down and join the fun! A throwback to family reads of yore, this epic follows a troubled boy and a host of hilariously vexed animals who must save a river before it’s dammed, so they can save themselves. Gabriel (“G” for short) is wasting away in the Abiddon County Juvenile Center when he’s introduced to the Shongunk River by his dying uncle. The river valley—trash-heaped but chock-full of mysteries and fish—wins G over. But, as G has learned, good things can’t last. The Shongunk is scheduled to be dammed by a local developer. In a matter of days, it will cease flowing, and all of the talkative creatures who live there in the river valley will be as homeless as G. Just as G decides it’s no time to accept his fate, so too do the animals. To inspire an uprising, a young trout is nominated to make a fateful journey up the river; a raccoon swears a violent oath against humans; and a newly sober buck leads his skittish flock out of harm’s way. Together with G, they show that good can triumph and that there is power in all of us, even the smallest minnow. KIRK LOMBARD is an author, angler, sustainable fishmonger, and tuba player who once worked inside the juvenile rehabilitation system. His first book, the award-winning Sea Forager’s Guide to the Northern California Coast , was described as “poetry” for fish by NPR. He lives in Half Moon Bay with his family, raising his children on herring and sea shanties.

DEMOLA the VIOLINIST BIO: Demola, known to fans as “Demola the Violinist,” is an internationally recognized musician, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist, record producer, and award-winning self-taught multi-genre violinist. Born in Lagos, Nigeria, Demola moved to the United States to pursue his solo music career, blending his love for Afrobeat, reggae, R&B, hip-hop, pop, and country into a sound that is distinctly his own. In 2024, Demola’s career reached new heights, fueled by his vibrant social media presence and viral performances. With over 6 million followers and millions of streams across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, his videos regularly attract millions of views, making him one of the most-followed and celebrated violinists worldwide. His performances captivate global audiences, and his fanbase continues to expand with each viral hit. This year, Demola launched his highly successful “One in a Million 2.0” tour, performing in over 20 cities and mesmerizing audiences with original songs like “ONE IN A MILLION,” “MBAPPE,” and “LOVA,” which have collectively amassed millions of streams. He also made waves with his feature on the song “FORGIVE OUR TRESPASSES,” showcasing viral Afrobeat across the US and performing at Coachella. A hometown hero in Houston, Texas, Demola, has performed the national anthem for major sports teams, including the Houston Astros, Rockets, Dynamo, and Texans, before crowds of up to 70,000 people. He has also shared the stage with country music star Jelly Roll, performing for 74,000 fans at the Houston Rodeo. Demola is a fan favorite on television as well, with appearances on Good Morning America Online, FOX 26 Houston, CultureMap Houston, 97.9 KBXX Houston, FOX 31 Denver, WGN-9 Chicago, Black News Channel, and many others. His innovative fusion of genres has made him one of the first artists of his kind, captivating listeners with the melodic beauty of his violin and proving that he is truly one in a million. 7568d7b0-1f3e-47d0-acf1-58a1de7fa74b: Throwin’ Bo’s presents: Dagmar Zuniga Nicaraguan-American artist Dagmar Zuniga makes music that feels both intimate and expansive: songs drift like disrupted signals, carried by harmony, tape hiss, and a strong sense of touch. Her debut solo album in filth your mystery is kingdom / far smile peasant in yellow music — written and recorded in New York, Norway, and Athens, Georgia over a period of five years on her longtime companion, the Tascam 424 — was released by the People’s Coalition of Tandy on Bandcamp & YouTube in January 2025, accompanied by a small tape run that sold out instantly. The project quickly garnered over two hundred thousand views and the attention of artists such as Mount Eerie, who invited her to tour with them that summer. This year, what was once a jewel of tapped-in algorithms and message boards will meet the world at large, with in filth arriving digitally on March 4 , and physically on April 10 , via AD 93 . in filth is an atmospheric, devotional collage where one voice multiplies into a chorus of selves, sometimes delicate, sometimes severe; an effect created by Zuniga’s masterful layering of texture and complex harmonies. Synths glitter out like spears of sunlight from beneath clouds of moody, time-distorted guitars, and songs spin about themselves like tightly-wound music boxes, making use of a kind of hypnotic repetition, before melting apart into their components or slipping into the following track. Zuniga began recording to tape as a teenager, drawn to the physicality of the medium — how a tape recording is fragile, mutable, and alive. Though her ethereal sound may draw easy comparisons to other female pioneers of psychedelic folk, she is influenced just as much by the darker sounds of Syd Barrett and The Fall. Like Barrett, Zuniga is a painter, and she is interested not only in recording music but in creating a full, self-contained artistic universe: she creates her own artwork, merchandise, music videos, and bootleg tapes of new and unfinished music that she exclusively sells at live shows ( “If something is not material, it does not exist,” she insists). Her world has not gone unvisited, garnering her a monthly show on NTS Radio ‘World of Pain’, as well as a forthcoming appearance at Rewire Festival in April 2026. Though Zuniga’s work explores themes of solitude and suffering, the suffering in her songs is not borrowed or displayed; it is held, then opened outward through empathy — an exacting practice of attention that insists on shared ground. Solitude, in her work, is not withdrawal but a starting point for connection. Likewise, over time, her recording process has become increasingly communal, with in filth featuring musicians across the globe. Newer recordings widen the circle even more. For Zuniga, collaboration is a way to “find a place between worlds,” echoing Badiou’s idea of love as a vision refracted through the prism of difference. Meaning emerges there — in the space between voices, between artist and listener. “I hope my music helps people work through difficult experiences,” she says. “The same way it helps me.” Bandcamp | IG Support to be announced DOORS at 7:00PM | MUSIC at 8:00 PM Tickets

It’s December of 1970 in East Oakland and six year old Brian Copeland wants to make his mother smile with a brand new jewelry box for Christmas. How can he possibly raise the needed $11.97 by Christmas Eve? Follow the hilarious, poignant journey of a determined child as he navigates the winos, mean landlords and shady used car salesmen of his rough urban neighborhood, as well as his abusive father to discover the true meaning of the season. Brian Copeland (performer) has been in show business since he first stepped on the comedy stage at the tender age of 18. Soon he was headlining clubs and concerts across the country and opening for such artists as Smokey Robinson, The Temptations, Ringo Starr, and the Queen of soul Aretha Franklin, in venues from The Universal Amphitheater to Constitution Hall in Washington DC. Soon, Copeland branched off into television, appearing on comedy programs on NBC, A&E and MTV. He spent five years as co-host of San Francisco FOX affiliate KTVU breakfast program Mornings on 2 and two years hosting San Francisco ABC affiliate KGO’s Emmy Award winning afternoon talker 7Live. In 1995, ABC affiliate KGO Radio premiered “The Brian Copeland Show”. Its unique mix of talk and entertainment soon made it the most listened to program in its time slot. Copeland branched out into theater in 2004 with his first solo play, NOT A GENUINE BLACK MAN. This critically acclaimed exploration of race and identity created an audience pleasing blend of laughter, tears and sociology that led to the show becoming the longest running solo play in San Francisco theatrical history. Successful runs in Los Angeles and Off Broadway and a bestselling book adaptation followed. GENUINE has been performed in over 30 cities across America. Copeland’s other theatrical work includes THE WAITING PERIOD, a solo play about his lifelong struggle with depression and Grandma & Me, which premiered in 2022 at The Marsh. David Ford (director) is a director, collaborator, and Goldie Award-winning playwright who has worked on countless solo shows over his 25-year career in the business. Frequently working on projects at The Marsh, Ford has collaborated with many Bay Area favorites including Charlie Varon, Marilyn Pitman, Geoff Hoyle and Cherry Terror.

Recommended for ages 6–10, parents, grandparents, teachers, and anyone who wants to remember what it feels like to live with curiosity, courage, humor, and heart. The Braunicles invite readers into the wonderfully imperfect world of a spirited little boy named Braun. A world filled with adventure, mischief, big feelings, unexpected lessons, and an irresistible enthusiasm for life. Written by Jennifer Levi, the stories are warm, funny, honest, and deeply human. Jennifer gives a distinctive voice and captures childhood in a way that feels both whimsical and completely real: the bold ideas, the questionable decisions, the enormous emotions, the funny family dynamics, and the little moments that often become the memories we treasure most. At its heart, The Braunicles is about living fully. Braun approaches the world with curiosity. He takes chances. He includes people. He makes mistakes. He loves fiercely. He finds fun where others might not see it. And through each story, young readers discover that some of the qualities that make a child challenging, surprising, loud, adventurous, or different can also become their greatest strengths. For parents and grandparents, there is another layer. These stories are a gentle reminder not to rush through childhood trying to make everything perfect. Sometimes the mess is the memory. Sometimes the mischievous child becomes the unforgettable adult. Sometimes the moments that make us shake our heads today are exactly the stories we will tell for the rest of our lives. Jennifer’s voice brings humor and perspective to parenting without preaching. That makes The Braunicles more than a children’s book. -It is a book children can enjoy for adventure. -It is a book parents can recognize themselves in. -It is a book grandparents can give with meaning. -And it is a book families can read together and talk about long after the final page. Jennifer Levi is the founder of The Live Like Braun Foundation and the force behind The Live Like Braun movement. Since the death of her son in May 2025, Jennifer has become a powerful advocate for DUI awareness and meaningful legislative change, passing a new Bill in CA, testifying at the CA State Capitol and on Capitol Hill. She regularly speaks to audiences at DUI workshops and schools all over Southern CA. She serves on MADD's CA State Legislative Board. Jennifer’s advocacy has been featured across multiple media outlets and television networks including NBC, ABC, Fox, and CBS, along with well-known podcasts hosted by Dr. Phil, Kennedy, Jason Kennedy, Amanda Kloots, Kelly Gores, Meghan Judge, and Kate Casey. Jennifer has spoken openly about the profound transformation of her life following the death of her son. She has become a featured contributor to Maria Shriver’s Sunday Paper, writing about the ways grief has reshaped her life with raw honesty, deep emotion, and a touch of irreverence. She hopes The Braunicles inspires children to embrace exactly who they are and encourages grown-ups to give young people the freedom to let their brightest, silliest, most authentic selves shine. Jennifer is a mother, wife, advocate, writer, and former TV executive. Although she has worn many hats, she has always said she is most proud of her role as mom to her two children, Adelle and Braun. She lives in Pacific Palisades, California, with her family and two very naughty dogs. That can feel painful or lonely when we’ve had meaningful journeys (and also when we’ve had disappointing journeys!). Healing – especially from interpersonal injuries – deepens when done in community. The same is true of personal and spiritual growth. 2c5ebbc8-b832-44d7-b506-ed7d6bfef162: (Please do not bring infants to the show) A hippie, activist, lesbian, feminist, lawyer, judge’s search for identity & justice. The at times humorous and at times deadly serious show begins when Amy moves to Berkeley in the early 1970’s during second wave feminism. Amy finds her identity as a lesbian feminist, goes to law school to fight for women’s rights, represents coal miners and battered women in Appalachia and returns to California to open a lesbian feminist law practice. She is representing women who had been sexually harassed – pre-Anita Hill – but keeps seeing all sides of things, becomes an administrative judge and starts a law firm to do mediation and impartial investigations of harassment and discrimination. She adopts two children – both biracial – and experiences racism up close and personal. In the meantime, she can’t stop revisiting her first experience with the criminal justice system in 1970 when she accompanied a friend to a rape trial. Her (white) friend had been raped by a (Black) boyfriend. The friend wanted him to get help, rather than serve a decade in prison. This restorative justice solution was not an option. Amy wonders about her role in the verdict and if real justice is possible in an unjust world. Content Advisories: The content of this production includes topics and events that may be triggering to some people including sexual violence/rape, sexual harassment, racism and familial violence.

f1965f6a-fbde-4018-9b39-36bd1b1b0ec8: Every Tuesday morning, the Alembic opens for a half-day of silent meditation practice. Participants are invited to bring and engage in their own silent meditation practice. Whether you practice mindfulness, Zen, Vipassana, contemplation, prayer, or another silent form of meditation, all are welcome. The retreat begins promptly at 9:30 AM and concludes at 11:50 AM. Please arrive between 9:15 AM and 9:25 AM to remove your shoes, settle in, and find a seat before the first bell. Conversation is permitted during breaks; however, we encourage participants to keep voices low, as some attendees choose to observe silence throughout the entire morning. You are welcome to leave the meditation hall at any time if needed. If you leave during a meditation period, please wait until the next break before re-entering. We provide the structure and the space; you provide your own silent practice. Participants may choose to sit in Sol or engage in quiet movement practice in the tearoom during meditation periods. Thank you for helping us maintain a quiet and supportive environment for practice.
1a182e64-fbd7-43ef-a8c0-d9875c5626ed: What is Bookagami? Book Folding is a global art genre. No glue, no scissors, no stress! Learn how to repurpose discarded (or favorite) books into beautiful, sculptural art with the award-winning Marin artist Adrienne Biggs, the originator behind Bookagami. This hands-on Bookagami workshop guides participants through the meditative and mindful practice of folding books into unique, creative, and sustainable art. Adrienne Biggs’ Bookagami art has captivated Marin . A 30-year Marin resident and former book publishing professional, Adrienne will introduce her unique approach—combining origami, altered books, and circular economy principles—to help every attendee fold up to three books into works of art. Workshop Highlights: Learn Bookagami techniques: Start with simple folds and progress to more complex forms, suitable for all skill levels. Embrace sustainability: Discover how book folding diverts unwanted books from the landfill and gives them renewed purpose. Connect and create: Enjoy a community atmosphere where creativity sparks joy and every fold is intentional yet also spontaneous. Take home your art: Finish the session with your handmade Bookagami sculptures to display at home or give as gifts, and the skills to keep folding. What to bring to the workshop: Newer paperbacks or hardcovers with minimum 1” spine (around 300 pages) work best. Books with words and books with images produce different results/color patterns, so you are encouraged to bring and try both at the workshop (see images below for examples). Book Passage can also supply you with books if needed. Meet Your Instructor Adrienne Biggs is an accomplished artist known for fostering creative inclinations within this community, while rescuing books from landfill (or a dusty bookshelf) by repurposing these common two-dimensional objects into three-dimensional works of art that people of all ages can enjoy, create, and share. Since 2024, she has created more than 600 unique “Bookagami” (as she calls them). Her Atlas, 1963: You Are Here won First Place Blue Ribbon at the 2024 Marin County Fair, and her Bug-a-Gami totem and her Stars, Stripes & Stories piece each won ribbons in 2025 and 2026. Past public art exhibits include two-month shows at Town Books in San Anselmo and at Marelli’s in downtown San Rafael; three month shows at the downtown San Rafael Public Library and at the Friends School in San Francisco; one-month show at ACCI Gallery in Berkeley; and various exhibits at ArtWorks Downtown in San Rafael. Her current solo show, Black White & Read All Over, is at Falkirk Cultural Center in San Rafael November 6 - December 15, 2026. Learn more at @IntoTheFoldBookagami on Instagram. She told fun stories and was very motivating. I had three great examples I created and brought home...I am not crafty and Bookagami was easy to do and fun to learn." Diana S.

683c59f8-a899-49a9-9a4b-c9cace076086: Who Gets to Tell the Story? · Every book on a shelf is the result of a series of choices. Which ideas are considered urgent? Which voices are given space? Who decides what gets published, how a book is positioned, who is imagined as its reader, and, ultimately, which books find their way into our hands? From the outside, publishing can look like a relatively straightforward journey: an idea becomes a manuscript, a manuscript becomes a book, a book arrives on a shelf. But behind that journey is an ecosystem of editors, publishers, marketers, distributors, booksellers, institutions, economics, relationships, taste, timing, and power. At every stage, someone is deciding what is worth paying attention to. Join us at Clio’s for a conversation about the politics of publishing with Tim McKee , Publisher of North Atlantic Books; Michelle Phan , Marketing Manager at University of California Press; author and advocate Kelechi Ubozoh ; and cultural anthropologist and Clio’s founding member Cari Borja , whose programming explores what can happen when different voices, disciplines, and ways of knowing are deliberately juxtaposed, creating the possibility for unlikely conversations. Together, we’ll follow a book from idea to bookshelf while asking the harder questions beneath that journey: Who gets through the door? What kinds of knowledge are valued? Which stories enter the cultural conversation, and which don’t? What gets changed, or lost along the way? And what roles do authors, publishers, marketers, booksellers, programmers, and readers play in determining which ideas circulate through our culture? Kelechi Ubozoh’s We’ve Been Too Patient: Voices from Radical Mental Health gives us a particularly powerful book through which to examine these questions. Bringing together voices challenging conventional understandings of mental health and healing, the anthology asks what happens when lived experience itself becomes a form of knowledge, and what it takes for voices outside dominant systems to make their way into print and into public conversation. A bookstore is never simply a place where books are sold. It is a place where voices are chosen, ideas are juxtaposed, unlikely conversations begin, and culture is made. Tim McKee, Publisher, North Atlantic Books Tim came to NAB in 2013 and is honored to serve as publisher. Born in New York City, McKee grew up in Los Angeles and received a BA from Princeton University and an MA in journalism from the University of Missouri. He has worked in the nonprofit sector for his entire career, including serving as the long-time managing editor of The Sun magazine, the grants director for a social-justice foundation in San Francisco, and as a writer for several community-based organizations in California. He has also taught college-level writing and journalism. His book No More Strangers Now: Young Voices from a New South Africa (Dorling Kindersley) was an Honor Book for the Jane Addams Book Award and a Los Angeles Times bestseller. He is happiest when bringing necessary stories to the page. Michelle Phan , Marketing Manager, UC Press Michelle launched her publishing career at North Atlantic Books as a publicist before transitioning to marketing at UC Press. With 7+ years of experience in book promotion, she is passionate about uplifting authors and books that share the knowledge necessary for our times. As Vice President of Bay Area Women in Publishing and Co-Chair of the Robin Seaman Award Committee, she also cares deeply about fostering meaningful relationships and building inclusive community within the industry. Kelechi Ubozoh, Author and advocate For over a decade, Kelechi has worked in the California mental health system in the areas of research and advocacy, community engagement, stigma reduction, youth development and peer support. Kelechi has spoken publicly about her experiences on multiple platforms, including CBS This Morning with Gayle King, O The Oprah Magazine, and The S Word documentary. Kelechi began her career as an investigative reporter in New York City, and was the first student-reporter ever published in The New York Times . In 2019, Kelechi published her anthology with L.D. Green, We’ve Been Too Patien t, which features diverse voices who all share their stories of radical healing and consider the recent movement towards reform in the mental health field, including the mad pride/consumer movement, theater as therapy, peer support, combating stigma, and trauma-informed care. Most recently, she co-authored What I Wish My People Had Known: The Psychiatric Green Book: A Guide for Black Folks with Yolo Akili Robinson, a strategic guide helping Black communities protect against racialized violence and institutional harm.

The Flying Death tells the story of how a modern-day miracle drug was born out of an Amazonian blowgun poison thanks to the efforts of a motley crew of fortune-seeking adventurers—a crew that included a handful of unscrupulous medical researchers, an obsessive White Russian émigré, and an American storyteller with big dreams.”—John Lee Anderson, author of Che: A Revolutionary Life Matt will be joined in conversation by Rebecca Herman, Associate Professor of History, U.C. Berkeley. In The Flying Death: Poison, Plunder, and the Quest for a Miracle Medicine in the Amazon (FSG; November 10, 2026), historian Matt O’Hara tells the story of a young, frail American explorer named Richard Gill, who traveled to the Amazon in the 1930s to open a tourist ranch. Instead, he stirred up an international hunt to harvest a local vine known as curare. As Gill and his rivals quickly realized, curare was both a dangerous poison used by local tribes in blow darts and a potential cure for numerous ailments, including multiple sclerosis and other motor diseases. Seeking to treat his own degenerative illness and make a fortune, Gill established connections with tribal leaders and pharmaceutical companies back home—even as his Russian-born rival, Boris Krukoff, sought to do the same. Navigating treacherous terrain and politics, Gill and Krukoff successfully created a veritable curare industrial complex. The plant became a key element in shock therapy treatments and, eventually, in anesthesia back in the United States. Gill and Krukoff’s rivalry and ethical compromises offer a timeless reflection on how personal ambition, competition, and obsession can shape—and sometimes distort—scientific and cultural progress. In this ethnobotanical adventure story, O’Hara deftly explores the intersections of indigenous knowledge, scientific exploration, and exploitation, and poses searching moral ​conundrums about the price of progress. And who pays it. “The Flying Death is as gripping as the exotic poison at its heart. Matt O’Hara is a master researcher who brews a tale at the frontiers of scientific discovery, with healthy doses of ambition and adventure mixed in. This is historical narrative nonfiction at its best.” —Mitchell Zuckoff, author of Lost in Shangri-La “Matt O’Hara has uncovered the thrilling true story of Richard Gill, a sickly American explorer who ventured into the Amazon in 1938—and ended up transforming medicine. Moving from jungle rivers and poison-masters to medical trials and corporate boardrooms, O’Hara offers a gripping, exciting, and deeply researched adventure story about ambition, exploitation, and the true cost of medical breakthroughs.”—Charles Duhigg, author of The Power of Habit “The Flying Death, Matt O’Hara’s brilliant tale of the South American poison curare, is a wild ride driven by courage, mystery, pharmaceutical wrongdoing, and Indigenous wisdom. The story will surprise you, infuriate you—and it will definitely make you smarter.” —Deborah Blum, author of The Poisoner’s Handbook “An unforgettable tale of medicine, ambition, greed, and the natural world, The Flying Death is a true page-turner. Matt O’Hara is a tenacious historian who writes with great skill and with a keen eye for human drama and injustice.”—Hector Tobar, author of Deep Down Dark Matt O’Hara is a professor of history at the University of California, Santa Cruz. He is the award-winning author of many journal articles and two books, The History of the Future in Colonial Mexico and A Flock Divided: Race, Religion, and Politics in Mexico, 1749–1857. Rebecca Herman is Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley, where she teaches about environmental politics, US-Latin American relations, and modern Latin America. She is the author of Cooperating with the Colossus: A Social and Political History of US Military Bases in World War II Latin America and is currently at work on a book about anti-extractivism in Antarctica. Her first novel, The Outposters, will be published next summer by Cardinal. 84e94840-8832-435a-b360-38f6bb59f6ee: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. He draws from a decade of experience guiding men’s circles, performance dance teams, applied AI research, and meditation. Some recent inspirations of his are Ego Development Theory, madhyamaka philosophy, and Brazilian zouk. He is known for his steady, compassionate presence and calibrated relational risk-taking. He works full-time at the intersection of mental health and AI as a machine learning researcher.

393bcee2-d3a0-4d39-994e-fda39c648035: Rebuilding Our Cities — And Our Democracy · Cities like New York, Los Angeles, and San Francisco are in crisis. Chronic housing shortages are driving countless middle-class and working-class households out of high-opportunity areas. Homelessness is skyrocketing. Cars continue to rule city streets, poisoning the climate and putting everyone’s health and safety at risk. And city governments, instead of rising to meet the challenge, are increasingly dysfunctional and unaccountable. Build or Die: How America Is Suffocating Its Cities and What to Do About It traces the history of a disaster a century in the making, detailing how shortsighted and reactionary policy decisions led to the interlocking crisis that threatens America’s great cities.Join Build or Die author Ned Resnikoff, California Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, and Economic Security Project co-founder Natalie Foster for a conversation about what ails America's great cities—and how we can revitalize both urban America and American democracy. Ned Resnikoff is an independent writer and urban policy analyst. His work has appeared in The New York Times , San Francisco Chronicle , The New Republic , The Nation , Dissent , and The Atlantic , among other publications. He writes Public Comment , an online newsletter about cities and democracy. Natalie Foster is author of The Guarantee: Inside the Fight For America’s Next Economy and co-founder and former President of Economic Security Project, an organization dedicated to building economic power for everyday Americans. She's a Senior Fellow at the Aspen Institute Future of Work Initiative.

4d3c6add-a153-431c-af92-04b5e4dd81d4: Embodiment Practices is an invitation to practice giving ourselves permission to arrive fully to where we are, and gently explore movement and stillness to care for our bodies and ourselves. This event happens each week at the Alembic. As an element of self attunement, we will practice making intuitive choices through a lens of self love, meaning that we are each making choices that are nourishing and responsive to ourselves as individuals in that moment. Part of this practice includes being very intentional and explicit about what kinds of choices we might consider, and being curious about how it feels to try them. There will be many options provided throughout, with guidance around how to navigate choice making, including if this is new to you or you are navigating a limitation or injury. There will be a corner of the room set aside in case you’d like to opt out of the facilitated structure and take a moment for yourself to rest. Opening Circle: We'll ground and check-in with whatever feels present for each of us. We get to welcome ourselves to come as we are. Warm Up: We'll do a guided, full-bodied warm up, tuning the instruments of our bodies and attention, giving ourselves time to shake it out, stretch, wiggle, and move through whatever feels stuck. Movements will be simple enough to follow along, giving us a chance to get out of our heads and drop into our bodies, regulating our nervous system. Drawing on contemporary dance and yoga, there will be flow, rhythm, and music. Movement Explorations: We'll explore movements that deepen our connection with our bodies and our intuition, focusing on concepts and areas of the body that can help us settle and release. Meditation: Finally, we'll settle into meditation and rest. Finding stillness might be sitting/standing/lying down and might include cozy props, having eyes open or closed, and suggestions to make yourself comfortable, including allowing some body movement within that quiet space. Please bring clothes you feel comfortable to move in. It’s recommended to bring long sleeves, long pants and socks with you, in case we are moving on the floor. Bring a journal if you’d like. About Suzanne (Zan): With three decades of contemporary/modern dance experience and 15 years of teaching, Suzanne Beahrs guides students in exploring movement as a pathway to deeper connection—with ourselves, our surroundings, and each other. Her classes blend technical training, creative expression, and guidance on being intentional with how we are each practicing. Her movement style was described by The New York Times as “grounded, silken.” In addition to contemporary dance, she is currently heavily influenced by house dance, contact improvisation, and mindfulness practices. She is currently on faculty at Shawl-Anderson Dance Center and teaches around the Bay Area, including ODC, the Berkeley Alembic, and Finnish Hall. Zan has previously taught extensively at Gibney, Elon University, ADF studios, and many more. It's a 9-song collection that's largely made up of bluesy, gothy, emo-y melancholic songs that sometimes sound like a cross between '90s Cure deep cuts and Nirvana Unplugged. (Lukas also cites Scott Walker as an influence, and you can hear that too.) Most of the album is bare-bones and somber, but Lukas also revs things up for the noise punk of "Faction from Under the Grove," and that fits right in too. With As We Pass, Lukas enters a long, line of depressive singer/songwriters, but even with over half a century of music like this, something about Lukas stands out. He grips you right off the bat with album opener "After the Alphabets" -- the kind of song that can make you drop everything and listen as soon as his voice comes in -- and the album stays that compelling throughout. Even with connections to established artists and the great Sargent House label behind him, this doesn't feel like the smash arrival of a hot new buzz artist; it's the subtle arrival of a songwriter whose songs creep up on you and knock you out when you're least expecting it. 07783702-7c5e-40b1-a0a7-792668035b21: When we gather with others, conversation almost automatically drifts toward what has already happened or what might happen next. Stories, plans, reactions, hopes—these patterns are so ingrained that we barely notice how completely we relate to one another through the lens of the past and future. But when we pause those habits, something surprising occurs. The room changes. Attention sharpens. A different kind of connection begins to emerge. A small clearing inside awareness opens—a place where no future is rehearsing itself, and no echoes of the past are allowed to enter. We can touch this space alone in contemplative practices, but it's rare to enter it with others. The Present Moment Game is a simple social meditation designed to explore that possibility. Participants speak only from what is happening in the moment, and gently bring each other back when attention drifts. What unfolds is often unexpected, and never the same twice. Curious? Come play! ___________ What to Expect 6:30 PM — Doors open Arrive anytime in the next 30 minutes. You’re welcome to enjoy tea as you settle in—just note that drinks won’t be brought into the circle, so come early if you’d like to enjoy an unrushed cup. 7:00 PM — The event begins This is a “sealed-container” experience. Out of care for the group, we can’t allow late entry, so please be sure to arrive between 6:30 and 7:00. After a brief grace period, doors will close at 7:05. 7:06 PM — Welcome, introductions & game rules A short orientation covering the simple guidelines. 7:25 PM — The Present Moment Game begins 8:25 PM — The game ends We’ll then move into group reflections. ~8:45 PM — Event concludes ___________ Is This Event for You? A few things to consider before you decide: Phones and watches off As an invitation to loosen your grip on time, you’ll be asked to remove your watch and fully power down your phone for the full duration of the experience. This is not an Authentic Relating practice T-Group, Circling, and other AR forms use present-moment awareness as a vehicle for relational exploration. That’s not what we’re doing here. Our subject isn’t each other, but the moment itself. Kindness is essential Please come willing to encounter everyone in the room with openness and warmth. This is a gentle space for contemplation and focused attention, not edge-pushing or confrontation. ___________ One participant’s experience: "As a person who loves, thinks and talks about language for a living, I am wide-eyed at how speaking solely in the present tense feels rich, alive and vital. It’s the best of meditation and conversation, distilled into an hour of social elixir; a stop-you-in-your-tracks nexus of collective mind. I feel hooked, thirsty for more. Alli creates a magical container. You won’t regret it." — Sophia ___________ About your host Alli Magidsohn is the creator of The Present Moment Game, an experimental social meditation that invites a small group to do something surprisingly rare: be fully present together, in real time. The idea grew out of Alli's experience with T-Group, a practice she found genuinely transformative. But as she went deeper, she became increasingly captivated by something specific: the quality of attention that arises when a group of people focus on what's actually happening, right now. That observation became a question: What if the present moment wasn’t just the context of a relationally-focused experience, but the primary subject of the inquiry itself? Drawing in part on the linguistic principles of E-Prime, she designed a set of simple constraints that gently guide conversation away from the past and future, and into the living moment. The result is something playful, quietly profound, and hard to describe until you experience it. CONFUNKSHUN The R&B funk icon, Confunkshun, who has been pleasing fans for over 50 years, is at it again! After the success of Love’s Train being rerecorded by Silk Sonic (Bruno Mars and Anderson Paak) and reaching #1 on the charts, the band’s locomotive has once again rolled out with recent singles Text Me Tomorrow and Smooth from their highly anticipated 2024 spring album release, Smooth Jukebox. Initially known as Project Soul, the R&B funk icon group we now know as Confunkshun has been pleasing fans for over 50 years. Originating in Vallejo, CA, founding member Michael Cooper, along with high school classmates Louis McCall, Karl Fuller, Cedric Martin, Danny Thomas, Paul “Zebulan” Harrell, and newfound talent Felton Pilate, started this unprecedented music journey. Eventually, the group found a home in Memphis in the mid-'70s when they booked a performance backing Stax Recording Artist the Soul Children. Soon, they were recruited as the background band for Rufus Thomas for the Golden Globe-nominated Wattstax Benefit Concert/ Documentary. While in pursuit of a recording contract, the group adopted a new name inspired by the group NiteLiters’ song, Confunkshun. The newly renamed act attracted the attention of Mercury Records, and soon set funkateers around the world on fire with their debut album featuring their first single “Sho'Feels Good To Me.” Confunkshun went on to release a total of 11 albums and eight top ten Billboard hits, including the No. 1 hit single “Ffun”, “Chase Me”, “Shake & Dance”, “Baby I’m Hooked”, and more. Ironically, their biggest hit was an album cut that was never released as a single. The fan favorite, Love’s Train, propelled Confunkshun’s “To the Max” album to Gold Status. But it was 40 years later that supergroup Silk Sonic’s remake of the single took it to #1 on the charts, helping the duo (Bruno Mars & Anderson Paak) win a BET Album of the Year Award. In 2022, Michael Cooper and Felton Pilate were presented with Honorary Doctorates of Humane Letters from the Christian Bible Institute, with Confunkshun member Dr. Ron Moton earning his Ph.D. In 2018, Confunkshun can proudly claim to be one of the only R&B Funk bands with three doctoral members! Dr. Cooper and Dr. Pilate were also honored to receive the Presidential Lifetime Achievement Awards for their lifetime of service through music and more. This prestigious award has been awarded to a select few Americans to recognize over 4,000 hours of extraordinary service. Confunkshun’s current lineup includes three original members, Michael Cooper, Felton Pilate, and Karl Fuller, as well as the talents of Kurt “KC” Clayton, Ron Moton, Aaron Green, Rene Escovedo, and Brian LaTour. Additional support includes the service of long-time road manager and travel agent Steve Sullivan & Master of Ceremonies (Conductor), Clarence Isadore. They continue to mesmerize audiences with magnetic performances on their worldwide 2023 Smooth Jukebox Tour. The group is also a frequent favorite on the Soul Train Cruise and Tom Joyner Cruise, and will soon be on the upcoming Keith Sweat’s Sweatfest in the Dominican Republic. Their contribution to R&B music was recognized in 2014 with the National R&B Music Society Lifetime Achievement Award. Confunkshun’s catalog of hits remains on worldwide radio playlists and in the hearts of their dedicated fans. Con Funk Shun has produced several hits throughout their career. Some of their most popular songs include: 1. Ffun: This song topped the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1978. 2. Shake and Dance with Me: This song reached No. 5 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1978. 3. Chase Me: This song peaked at No. 4 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1979. 4. Got to Be Enough: This song reached No. 8 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1980. 5. Too Tight: This song peaked at No. 8 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1981. 6. Baby, I’m Hooked (Right into Your Love): This song reached No. 5 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1983. 7. Electric Lady: This song peaked at No. 4 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1985

CONFUNKSHUN The R&B funk icon, Confunkshun, who has been pleasing fans for over 50 years, is at it again! After the success of Love’s Train being rerecorded by Silk Sonic (Bruno Mars and Anderson Paak) and reaching #1 on the charts, the band’s locomotive has once again rolled out with recent singles Text Me Tomorrow and Smooth from their highly anticipated 2024 spring album release, Smooth Jukebox. Initially known as Project Soul, the R&B funk icon group we now know as Confunkshun has been pleasing fans for over 50 years. Originating in Vallejo, CA, founding member Michael Cooper, along with high school classmates Louis McCall, Karl Fuller, Cedric Martin, Danny Thomas, Paul “Zebulan” Harrell, and newfound talent Felton Pilate, started this unprecedented music journey. Eventually, the group found a home in Memphis in the mid-'70s when they booked a performance backing Stax Recording Artist the Soul Children. Soon, they were recruited as the background band for Rufus Thomas for the Golden Globe-nominated Wattstax Benefit Concert/ Documentary. While in pursuit of a recording contract, the group adopted a new name inspired by the group NiteLiters’ song, Confunkshun. The newly renamed act attracted the attention of Mercury Records, and soon set funkateers around the world on fire with their debut album featuring their first single “Sho'Feels Good To Me.” Confunkshun went on to release a total of 11 albums and eight top ten Billboard hits, including the No. 1 hit single “Ffun”, “Chase Me”, “Shake & Dance”, “Baby I’m Hooked”, and more. Ironically, their biggest hit was an album cut that was never released as a single. The fan favorite, Love’s Train, propelled Confunkshun’s “To the Max” album to Gold Status. But it was 40 years later that supergroup Silk Sonic’s remake of the single took it to #1 on the charts, helping the duo (Bruno Mars & Anderson Paak) win a BET Album of the Year Award. In 2022, Michael Cooper and Felton Pilate were presented with Honorary Doctorates of Humane Letters from the Christian Bible Institute, with Confunkshun member Dr. Ron Moton earning his Ph.D. In 2018, Confunkshun can proudly claim to be one of the only R&B Funk bands with three doctoral members! Dr. Cooper and Dr. Pilate were also honored to receive the Presidential Lifetime Achievement Awards for their lifetime of service through music and more. This prestigious award has been awarded to a select few Americans to recognize over 4,000 hours of extraordinary service. Confunkshun’s current lineup includes three original members, Michael Cooper, Felton Pilate, and Karl Fuller, as well as the talents of Kurt “KC” Clayton, Ron Moton, Aaron Green, Rene Escovedo, and Brian LaTour. 14bff46d-bcf5-4441-b493-8060d4cb084f: Throwin’ Bo’s presents: June McDoom There is a hush most of us only knew as children, the warm drift between familiar household sounds and being carried to bed, a place that belongs to you and to some self you have not met yet. June McDoom's debut full-length, Follow the Light, lives in that dream space and then keeps walking, slipping out of time and waking somewhere new, barely familiar enough to feel like home yet wholly your own. She came up in a Jamaican household on the edge of the Florida Everglades, an existence built of extended family, communal care, bass and harmonics. Her father, a carpenter and a student of sound, built his own speakers and kept three sound systems going across as many rooms. His low end would rise through her bedroom floor like some wayward cat while she lay above it with folk records, finding harmonies that were new and hers alone. Two musics in one room. Lushness as past and premonition. She found folk on her own, somewhere between the cast recording of The Sound of Music and Simon and Garfunkel, while everyone around her called it sleepy music. She did not mind being the only one. The solitude let her fall for harmony first, before words, before anything else, and harmony is still the thing she reaches for. Generationally speaking, the music was already in the air. Her grandfather, Colin Smith, is a distinguished mento man who played banjo and guitar and built his own rumba boxes, worked to keep Jamaica's oldest acoustic folk form alive. Mento is the root of all of it: ska, rock steady, reggae, dub and everything after. He is the one who put a guitar in her hands. An inheritance, a gift and a map. Even her name is part of it, though she will tell you she landed on it more by feel than reason. She records as June McDoom, born Alyssa, June being a nickname one of her grandmothers, Joan, went by, a name she thought was cool to carry and simply liked the sound of. An etheric channel that reverberates all the same. A dub all its own. Made slowly and by hand with her longtime partner Evan Wright, Follow the Light lays the harmony of folk over the rhythm of dub, with Dionne Warwick, Minnie Riperton, Pentangle and the washed guitars of Cocteau Twins haunting its outer edges. Voice and guitar seeking each other out first, then everything else stacked across long days in the studio they keep at home, restraint kept on purpose. The lead single "Without You" is the whole method surfacing, split open and sparkling like a geode in a creek bed. Angelic heroics, and nothing less. At the heart is family. Her grandmother Aggie, the light behind "Memory," guiding still. And underneath, the quieter truth the record keeps: none of us are only one person, but a continuum of selves, the ones who shaped us and the ones we have yet to meet. Future you is an ancestor your current self gets to greet. Press play and the same invitation is yours: A few minutes out of time, a place that turns familiar the longer you stay until you surface somewhere new and find it was yours all along. 6d6a456e-41a1-44f1-94af-45d0a3a594cb: (Please do not bring infants to the show) A hippie, activist, lesbian, feminist, lawyer, judge’s search for identity & justice. The at times humorous and at times deadly serious show begins when Amy moves to Berkeley in the early 1970’s during second wave feminism. Amy finds her identity as a lesbian feminist, goes to law school to fight for women’s rights, represents coal miners and battered women in Appalachia and returns to California to open a lesbian feminist law practice. She is representing women who had been sexually harassed – pre-Anita Hill – but keeps seeing all sides of things, becomes an administrative judge and starts a law firm to do mediation and impartial investigations of harassment and discrimination. She adopts two children – both biracial – and experiences racism up close and personal. In the meantime, she can’t stop revisiting her first experience with the criminal justice system in 1970 when she accompanied a friend to a rape trial. Her (white) friend had been raped by a (Black) boyfriend. The friend wanted him to get help, rather than serve a decade in prison. This restorative justice solution was not an option. Amy wonders about her role in the verdict and if real justice is possible in an unjust world. Content Advisories: The content of this production includes topics and events that may be triggering to some people including sexual violence/rape, sexual harassment, racism and familial violence.

CONFUNKSHUN The R&B funk icon, Confunkshun, who has been pleasing fans for over 50 years, is at it again! After the success of Love’s Train being rerecorded by Silk Sonic (Bruno Mars and Anderson Paak) and reaching #1 on the charts, the band’s locomotive has once again rolled out with recent singles Text Me Tomorrow and Smooth from their highly anticipated 2024 spring album release, Smooth Jukebox. Initially known as Project Soul, the R&B funk icon group we now know as Confunkshun has been pleasing fans for over 50 years. Originating in Vallejo, CA, founding member Michael Cooper, along with high school classmates Louis McCall, Karl Fuller, Cedric Martin, Danny Thomas, Paul “Zebulan” Harrell, and newfound talent Felton Pilate, started this unprecedented music journey. Eventually, the group found a home in Memphis in the mid-'70s when they booked a performance backing Stax Recording Artist the Soul Children. Soon, they were recruited as the background band for Rufus Thomas for the Golden Globe-nominated Wattstax Benefit Concert/ Documentary. While in pursuit of a recording contract, the group adopted a new name inspired by the group NiteLiters’ song, Confunkshun. The newly renamed act attracted the attention of Mercury Records, and soon set funkateers around the world on fire with their debut album featuring their first single “Sho'Feels Good To Me.” Confunkshun went on to release a total of 11 albums and eight top ten Billboard hits, including the No. 1 hit single “Ffun”, “Chase Me”, “Shake & Dance”, “Baby I’m Hooked”, and more. Ironically, their biggest hit was an album cut that was never released as a single. The fan favorite, Love’s Train, propelled Confunkshun’s “To the Max” album to Gold Status. But it was 40 years later that supergroup Silk Sonic’s remake of the single took it to #1 on the charts, helping the duo (Bruno Mars & Anderson Paak) win a BET Album of the Year Award. In 2022, Michael Cooper and Felton Pilate were presented with Honorary Doctorates of Humane Letters from the Christian Bible Institute, with Confunkshun member Dr. Ron Moton earning his Ph.D. In 2018, Confunkshun can proudly claim to be one of the only R&B Funk bands with three doctoral members! Dr. Cooper and Dr. Pilate were also honored to receive the Presidential Lifetime Achievement Awards for their lifetime of service through music and more. This prestigious award has been awarded to a select few Americans to recognize over 4,000 hours of extraordinary service. Confunkshun’s current lineup includes three original members, Michael Cooper, Felton Pilate, and Karl Fuller, as well as the talents of Kurt “KC” Clayton, Ron Moton, Aaron Green, Rene Escovedo, and Brian LaTour. Additional support includes the service of long-time road manager and travel agent Steve Sullivan & Master of Ceremonies (Conductor), Clarence Isadore. They continue to mesmerize audiences with magnetic performances on their worldwide 2023 Smooth Jukebox Tour. The group is also a frequent favorite on the Soul Train Cruise and Tom Joyner Cruise, and will soon be on the upcoming Keith Sweat’s Sweatfest in the Dominican Republic. Their contribution to R&B music was recognized in 2014 with the National R&B Music Society Lifetime Achievement Award. Confunkshun’s catalog of hits remains on worldwide radio playlists and in the hearts of their dedicated fans. Con Funk Shun has produced several hits throughout their career. Some of their most popular songs include: 1. Ffun: This song topped the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1978. 2. Shake and Dance with Me: This song reached No. 5 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1978. 3. Chase Me: This song peaked at No. 4 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1979. 4. Got to Be Enough: This song reached No. 8 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1980. 5. Too Tight: This song peaked at No. 8 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1981. 6. Baby, I’m Hooked (Right into Your Love): This song reached No. 5 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1983. 7. Electric Lady: This song peaked at No. 4 on the U.S. Billboard black singles chart in 1985
5fb9def0-e6b8-4efa-8ebc-6b92f2dd0dff: Ella Dair is a NYC-based jazz vocalist. Originally from San Francisco, she started singing at a young age, performing with many Bay Area legends in her aunt’s swing band “Lavay Smith & Her Red Hot Skillet Lickers.” Ella continued her education in music and performance with SFArtsEd, falling in love with the songs of Harold Arlen and Kander & Ebb, among other classics of the Great American Songbook. As a teenager she was a vocal soloist with the youth choir at Glide Memorial, the renowned non-denominational church presided over by civil rights leader Cecil Williams. Ella earned her bachelor’s degree from Bard College, studying anthropology and Latin American studies with a particular interest in ethnomusicology. Her studies broadened her musical tastes and sent her to Mexico City, where she lived post-grad. Ella then moved to New York City, joining the staff at Dizzy’s Club at Jazz At Lincoln Center, where she has been exposed to many of the greatest jazz musicians in the world. On her regular trips to the West Coast Ella performs at The Royal Cuckoo Organ Lounge in San Francisco, an iconic institution that has received rave reviews from the New York Times and the San Francisco Chronicle. At the Royal Cuckoo, Ella has sung with Etta James’ trumpet player Mike Olmos, Lyle Lovett’s alto player Brad Leali, and tenor saxophonist Howard Wiley, a resident Artistic Director at the SFJAZZ Center. Ella covers a range of material, including jazz standards, soul, country and folk tunes. She has a keen eye for unique and beautiful songs, and she continues to work tirelessly on expanding her repertoire, always on the lookout for obscure gems in addition to timeless classics.

0fafea4e-8218-49d1-80ec-1a65619c2cf7: October Theme: “Broadway and Show Tunes” There’s nothing that brings people together better than singing our favorite songs. It recalls summer nights around the campfire: someone strumming the guitar and all singing a mix of folk music, familiar songs we heard on the radio, and occasional new songs that someone shares. Nobody has to worry about whether you know the songs or can sing like a pro. This is our chance to share the joy of singing simply for the fun of it. Cary Sheldon is a singer, songwriter, and beloved Berkeley voice teacher with 30 years worth of grateful students. She has been playing and teaching in the Bay Area for the last 40 years. Her love for R & B music led her to be part of Zazu Pitts Memorial Orchestra in the 1980’s. Other affiliations include The Henry Kaiser Band, The Henriettas (a recreation of DeZurick sisters, a popular country music duo from the 1940’s), who appeared on Prairie Home Companion, and most recently her band DanceChant, a joyful community-inspired R&B band that encourages audience participation. She continues to be inspired by her love of singing in community. “Singing together with others is one of the greatest joys in my life.” Now in her 60’s, she returns to influences from her early life. Her grade school music teachers included John Langstaff, creator of the Christmas Revels, and the repertoire was based on the American folk tradition, including old English ballads, spirituals, freedom songs, and the popular folk and protest songs of the 1960’s. She hopes to inspire others to explore the depth of this material and rediscover the joy of community singing. Soprano Candace Johnson has led AMN’s Juneteenth Choral Celebration since its inception in 2020. The AMN community knows her through her commitment to the power of the Negro Spirituals tradition, but Candace has a deep connection to theater and to the music of the Broadway stage. A voice instructor at UC Berkeley for 17 years, in 2022 Candace also became the director of the University Gospel Choir. A lyric coloratura soprano, she crosses musical boundaries performing classical, jazz, musical theater, pop and gospel. She has sung on many stages, including Carnegie Hall and The Manhattan Center. Also a playwright and actress, Candace premiered her first one-woman show, Vox in a Box , in UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall in 2018, which led to her becoming a resident solo artist at The Marsh theater (Berkeley/San Francisco). Candace has written and performed 5 full-length one-woman musicals. Her most recent show, Scat-ter Brain: The Music of ADHD , was commissioned by The Marsh in 2024 for its inaugural IFOYE festival of new works by women-identifying playwrights. Following an extended run, Scat-ter Brain was nominated by Broadway World SF for Best Solo Show of 2025. Please read our Health, Safety and COVID-19 Information Our commitment to our patrons
8db47b76-6c1d-41c0-81f0-2585f2075b3b: FEAT. DENNIS CHAMBERS, DENNIS GWIZDALA, BOB FRANCESCHINI & LENI STERN · Legendary Guitarist Mike Stern On Tour! Mike Stern’s Debut Release With Mack Avenue Music Group/Artistry Music Features Collaborations With Christian McBride, Chris Potter, Antonio Sanchez, Dennis Chambers and Richard Bona Produced By The Late Jim Beard, Stern’s Longtime Collaborator and Friend Mike Stern's new album Echoes, And Other Songs marks his debut release on Mack Avenue Music Group/Artistry Music. Echoes delivers all the elements that longtime Stern fans want, and then some: the hook-filled rapid-fire bebop writing; the gorgeous melodic sensibility culled from African music, gospel and other influences; the breakneck improvisations that pepper hornlike bop virtuosity with rock fire. Along with the announcement, Stern has shared the lead single “Stuff Happens,” which features the 9-time Grammy Award winner Christian McBride . “It’s definitely got a Blues vibe, and it opens with a short but really wonderful solo from Christian McBride,” Stern says of the track. “He is definitely not only one of the greatest upright bass players ever, but he plays amazing electric bass. Of course, I knew that going into this project, so I asked him to play a lot of electric bass and he did that so beautifully on this tune. He played great on everything.” Stern has been celebrated for his versatile playing style since he first hit the scene in the 1970s, transcending genres by performing with Blood, Sweat & Tears, Miles Davis, Jaco Pastorius, The Brecker Brothers, David Sanborn, Béla Fleck, Yellowjackets and more. With Echoes and Other Songs, Stern brings together an all-star group of musicians, including Christian McBride, Chris Potter, Antonio Sanchez, Richard Bona & Dennis Chambers, for 11 brand-new originals that will captivate and unite guitar and jazz fans of all generations. This is Stern’s first release since the loss of longtime producer and keyboardist Jim Beard (who played on and produced the album), the closure of Stern’s beloved 55 Bar, and his 2016 injury, from which he continues to face physical hurdles. Echoes and Other Songs is a powerhouse document from one of the finest guitarists in jazz history, at a time in his career when he overcame immense physical struggles and experienced profound loss. In the sheer might of these performances, Echoes is a defiant record — not so much a victory lap as a call to arms. Echoes and Other Songs could be considered a loving farewell to Jim Beard, who passed away in March 2024. Beard acted as Stern’s go-to producer for over three decades, and as a favorite keyboardist for even longer. “I’m not exaggerating when I call Jim Beard a genius,” Stern says. “People would say, ‘You should change up your producer — you know, just mix it up.’ And I would say, ‘Why?’ Everybody loved Jim. He was just great at what he did — how he used technology, how he produced, how he mixed.” Stern goes on to describe Beard’s touch as a player. “Incredible.” He pauses. “Ridiculous… Everything he did was perfect. The records he came out with were amazing, but I think he could have done even more as a piano player.” In the end, though, Stern was most affected by Beard’s devotion as a friend. “When I had the blues,” he recalls, “when I felt low and wanted to talk to somebody, he’s one of the people I would reach out to. It would be short, but he would know exactly what I was talking about. It’s a heartbreaker.” Echoes also marks the first album Stern has released as a leader since the West Village jazz haunt 55 Bar closed its doors in 2022, a casualty of the pandemic. Stern’s regular gig there was legendary, enduring and advantageous; it was at 55 where Michael Brecker became interested in hiring the guitarist. His 55 residency also provided a physical-therapy regimen of sorts after Stern broke both of his humerus bones in 2016. He stumbled over construction materials on the street in New York and fell, and the aftermath included potentially career-ending nerve damage that threatened his picking hand. The road to recovery has been long, hard, and ongoing. Stern has had the abiding support of his wife, Leni, to help him, as well as godsends like Dr. Alton Barron, an orthopedic hand specialist recommended by a friend, fellow guitar master Wayne Krantz. Advised by another pal, the drummer Ray Levier, Stern came up with an efficient system for holding his pick, using wig glue and tape. “It was a challenge and a half,” Stern says, “and it still is, sometimes, just to accept it. It gets me really upset and frustrated because I used to play stuff with my fingers. I had to change certain things about my technique.” But Stern pushes on and rises above, as he has throughout his career — like when he rejoined Miles Davis’ band in 1985, having found sobriety. Throughout Echoes, you’d be hard-pressed to find a second in which Stern’s chops are less than sublime. In terms of expressivity, his flatpicking has no limitations. “I’m gonna keep trying with whatever I got,” Stern says. “You know I got to. Because I love it, and love means that some days you hate it; those two sides are on the same coin. But the love is definitely winning out.” Consider Mike Stern’s Echoes and Other Songs his love letter to jazz, to the guitar, to bandstand camaraderie, and to his own undefeated will. Echoes And Other Songs tracklist: 1. Connections 2. Echoes 3. Stuff Happens 4. Space Bar 5. I Hope So 6. Where’s Leo 7. Gospel Song 8. Crumbles 9. Curtis 10. Climate 11. 07bb0522-de82-4935-b3a7-dcf0b2814d9c: Every Tuesday morning, the Alembic opens for a half-day of silent meditation practice. This is an unguided silent retreat consisting of three 40-minute meditation periods. There will be no teacher-led instruction during the meditation periods. Participants are invited to bring and engage in their own silent meditation practice. Whether you practice mindfulness, Zen, Vipassana, contemplation, prayer, or another silent form of meditation, all are welcome. The retreat begins promptly at 9:30 AM and concludes at 11:50 AM. Please arrive between 9:15 AM and 9:25 AM to remove your shoes, settle in, and find a seat before the first bell. The morning is divided into three periods of silent meditation: 9:30 AM – 10:10 AM 10:20 AM – 11:00 AM 11:10 AM – 11:50 AM A bell will signal the beginning and end of each meditation period. The meditation hall (Sol) is reserved for silent practice during sitting periods. Between sits, participants may quietly stretch, visit the restroom, or spend time in the tearoom. Conversation is permitted during breaks; however, we encourage participants to keep voices low, as some attendees choose to observe silence throughout the entire morning. You are welcome to leave the meditation hall at any time if needed. If you leave during a meditation period, please wait until the next break before re-entering. We ask that all entrances and exits be as quiet and unobtrusive as possible. This is a “Bring Your Own Silent Meditation” retreat. We provide the structure and the space; you provide your own silent practice. Participants may choose to sit in Sol or engage in quiet movement practice in the tearoom during meditation periods. To minimize disruption, please enter Sol only during the transition periods between sits. If you arrive after a meditation period has begun, you are welcome to practice elsewhere in the Alembic until the next bell. The suggested donation is $10. No one will be turned away for lack of funds. We do ask that all attendees register through the Momence app or via the registration link on the Alembic website. Please note that the retreat ends at 11:50 AM, and we ask all participants to depart by 12:00 PM so that our volunteer teacher and staff may close the space in a timely manner. Thank you for helping us maintain a quiet and supportive environment for practice.
0fc3c8be-3913-43f9-88d8-e02c0fbe350f: In this deeply experiential yoga practice, we will explore the dynamic interplay between stability and mobility, strength and relaxation, movement and stillness. Through mindful movement, standing and seated practices, breath, and attention to the subtle ways we organize ourselves in space, we'll investigate what allows us to feel both grounded and free. This event happens each week at the Alembic. Rather than striving for perfect alignment or mastering difficult poses, we'll approach the practice as an exploration. We'll slow down enough to notice, experiment with different possibilities, and discover how the balance between effort and ease can change our experience of movement — and of ourselves.. Teacher Bio: Vickie Russell Bell has been teaching yoga for more than 30 years, bringing together the precision of alignment-based yoga with a deep curiosity about how we inhabit our bodies, regulate our nervous systems, and move through the world. She is an E-RYT 500 and Certified Yoga Therapist (C-IAYT), and has studied with some of the most respected teachers in the Iyengar-influenced yoga tradition. Her teaching is grounded in the belief that yoga is less about mastering poses than developing a more intimate relationship with ourselves. Her classes invite students to slow down, pay attention, and explore the constantly shifting relationships between stability and mobility, strength and softness, effort and ease. She teaches students of all ages and abilities, with a particular interest in yoga as a practice for living fully and well over time.

b8a65eb9-d047-4545-a9d3-f814caeb7085: FEAT. DENNIS CHAMBERS, DENNIS GWIZDALA, BOB FRANCESCHINI & LENI STERN · Legendary Guitarist Mike Stern On Tour! Mike Stern’s Debut Release With Mack Avenue Music Group/Artistry Music Features Collaborations With Christian McBride, Chris Potter, Antonio Sanchez, Dennis Chambers and Richard Bona Produced By The Late Jim Beard, Stern’s Longtime Collaborator and Friend Mike Stern's new album Echoes, And Other Songs marks his debut release on Mack Avenue Music Group/Artistry Music. Echoes delivers all the elements that longtime Stern fans want, and then some: the hook-filled rapid-fire bebop writing; the gorgeous melodic sensibility culled from African music, gospel and other influences; the breakneck improvisations that pepper hornlike bop virtuosity with rock fire. Along with the announcement, Stern has shared the lead single “Stuff Happens,” which features the 9-time Grammy Award winner Christian McBride . “It’s definitely got a Blues vibe, and it opens with a short but really wonderful solo from Christian McBride,” Stern says of the track. “He is definitely not only one of the greatest upright bass players ever, but he plays amazing electric bass. Of course, I knew that going into this project, so I asked him to play a lot of electric bass and he did that so beautifully on this tune. He played great on everything.” Stern has been celebrated for his versatile playing style since he first hit the scene in the 1970s, transcending genres by performing with Blood, Sweat & Tears, Miles Davis, Jaco Pastorius, The Brecker Brothers, David Sanborn, Béla Fleck, Yellowjackets and more. With Echoes and Other Songs, Stern brings together an all-star group of musicians, including Christian McBride, Chris Potter, Antonio Sanchez, Richard Bona & Dennis Chambers, for 11 brand-new originals that will captivate and unite guitar and jazz fans of all generations. This is Stern’s first release since the loss of longtime producer and keyboardist Jim Beard (who played on and produced the album), the closure of Stern’s beloved 55 Bar, and his 2016 injury, from which he continues to face physical hurdles. Echoes and Other Songs is a powerhouse document from one of the finest guitarists in jazz history, at a time in his career when he overcame immense physical struggles and experienced profound loss. In the sheer might of these performances, Echoes is a defiant record — not so much a victory lap as a call to arms. Echoes and Other Songs could be considered a loving farewell to Jim Beard, who passed away in March 2024. Beard acted as Stern’s go-to producer for over three decades, and as a favorite keyboardist for even longer. “I’m not exaggerating when I call Jim Beard a genius,” Stern says. “People would say, ‘You should change up your producer — you know, just mix it up.’ And I would say, ‘Why?’ Everybody loved Jim. He was just great at what he did — how he used technology, how he produced, how he mixed.” Stern goes on to describe Beard’s touch as a player. “Incredible.” He pauses. “Ridiculous… Everything he did was perfect. The records he came out with were amazing, but I think he could have done even more as a piano player.” In the end, though, Stern was most affected by Beard’s devotion as a friend. “When I had the blues,” he recalls, “when I felt low and wanted to talk to somebody, he’s one of the people I would reach out to. It would be short, but he would know exactly what I was talking about. It’s a heartbreaker.” Echoes also marks the first album Stern has released as a leader since the West Village jazz haunt 55 Bar closed its doors in 2022, a casualty of the pandemic. Stern’s regular gig there was legendary, enduring and advantageous; it was at 55 where Michael Brecker became interested in hiring the guitarist. His 55 residency also provided a physical-therapy regimen of sorts after Stern broke both of his humerus bones in 2016. He stumbled over construction materials on the street in New York and fell, and the aftermath included potentially career-ending nerve damage that threatened his picking hand. The road to recovery has been long, hard, and ongoing. Stern has had the abiding support of his wife, Leni, to help him, as well as godsends like Dr. Alton Barron, an orthopedic hand specialist recommended by a friend, fellow guitar master Wayne Krantz. Advised by another pal, the drummer Ray Levier, Stern came up with an efficient system for holding his pick, using wig glue and tape. “It was a challenge and a half,” Stern says, “and it still is, sometimes, just to accept it. It gets me really upset and frustrated because I used to play stuff with my fingers. I had to change certain things about my technique.” But Stern pushes on and rises above, as he has throughout his career — like when he rejoined Miles Davis’ band in 1985, having found sobriety. Throughout Echoes, you’d be hard-pressed to find a second in which Stern’s chops are less than sublime. In terms of expressivity, his flatpicking has no limitations. “I’m gonna keep trying with whatever I got,” Stern says. “You know I got to. Because I love it, and love means that some days you hate it; those two sides are on the same coin. But the love is definitely winning out.” Consider Mike Stern’s Echoes and Other Songs his love letter to jazz, to the guitar, to bandstand camaraderie, and to his own undefeated will. Echoes And Other Songs tracklist: 1. Connections 2. Echoes 3. Stuff Happens 4. Space Bar 5. I Hope So 6. Where’s Leo 7. Gospel Song 8. Crumbles 9. Curtis 10. Climate 11.
